issues.title: Extension-registered providers: fresh sessions intermittently ignore defaultProvider/defaultModel and start on another provider's default

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### What happened?

A fresh pi session intermittently does **not** start with the configured
`defaultProvider`/`defaultModel` from settings.json when that provider is
registered by an extension via `pi.registerProvider(name, config)`. Instead, pi
silently falls back to another provider's default model
(`defaultModelPerProvider`) — in our case `google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview`,
which our Google credential (free tier, quota `limit: 0`) cannot serve, so the
first request fails with a 429.

Measured over repeated fresh launches: ~4 of 10 sessions start on the wrong
model; the rest start correctly on the configured default. Instrumenting
`findInitialModel` (step 3) shows the outcome correlates 1:1 with the
availability snapshot state at resolution time:

```text
step3 <default-provider>/<default-model> -> HIT auth=false  → session starts on the fallback
step3 <default-provider>/<default-model> -> HIT auth=true   → session starts on the configured default
```

Root cause: `createAgentSession` resolves the initial model
(`restoreModelFromSession` / `findInitialModel`) before name+config provider
registrations from extensions are applied to the model registry.

- `pi.registerProvider(name, config)` queues into
  `runtime.pendingProviderRegistrations` while extensions are loading
  (loader.js, "Pre-bind: queue registrations…"); the queue is flushed in
  `bindCore`, which runs when the `AgentSession` is constructed — after
  initial model resolution.
- `findInitialModel` step 3 (model-resolver.js) requires
  `getModel(provider, id)` **and** `hasConfiguredAuth(provider)`; the latter
  reads `snapshot.configuredProviders`, which is rebuilt asynchronously by
  `runAvailabilityRefresh` and can lag the registration.
- When step 3 misses, step 4 returns the first `defaultModelPerProvider`
  match from the available snapshot — silently, with no warning.

Note that `pi.registerNativeProvider(provider)` (object form) is flushed in
`createAgentSessionServices` _with_ an awaited
`modelRuntime.refresh({ allowNetwork: false })` before model resolution — the
name+config form has no equivalent before `findInitialModel`.

Possibly a residual of #6948 / #6922 (async provider model refresh vs startup
resolution, addressed for the built-in llama.cpp provider): model lists now
hydrate from the store at startup, but the configured/auth snapshot can still
lag, and the fallback is silent instead of an error. #2291 is an earlier
instance of the same ordering problem from a `session_start` hook.

Suggested direction: after extension loading completes, flush both pending
registration queues (`name+config` and native) and await
`modelRuntime.refresh({ allowNetwork: false })` before initial-model
resolution — mirroring what `createAgentSessionServices` already does after
extension load. Happy to send a PR if the direction looks right.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Register a provider from an extension using the name+config form:

```ts
export default function (pi) {
  pi.registerProvider("acme", {
    name: "acme",
    baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:9/v1", // never called in this repro
    api: "openai-completions",
    models: [
      {
        id: "acme-model",
        name: "Acme Model",
        contextWindow: 128000,
        maxTokens: 8192,
      },
    ],
    auth: {
      apiKey: {
        name: "acme",
        check: async () => ({ type: "api_key" }),
        resolve: async () => ({ auth: { apiKey: "demo" }, source: "acme" }),
      },
    },
    fetchModels: async () => [],
  });
}
```

2. Add a stored credential for it in auth.json:

```json
"acme": { "type": "api_key", "key": "demo" }
```

3. settings.json:

```json
{ "defaultProvider": "acme", "defaultModel": "acme-model" }
```

4. Launch several fresh sessions back-to-back and inspect each session
   journal's first `model_change` entry:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  d=/tmp/repro-$i; mkdir -p "$d"; (cd "$d" && pi -p "hi" >/dev/null 2>&1)
done
# first model_change per journal: acme-model @ acme on good launches,
# gemini-3.1-pro-preview @ google on fallback launches
```

Measured: 4 of 10 fresh sessions started on the fallback provider; 10 of 10
with the refresh applied before resolution started on the configured default.

### Expected behavior

Every fresh session starts with `defaultProvider`/`defaultModel` from
settings.json — regardless of how long extension loading takes. If the
configured provider cannot be resolved yet, pi should say so explicitly
instead of silently starting on an unrelated provider's default model.

### Version

0.84.4

issues.title: Prompt template arguments drop apostrophes and merge words

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
### What happened?

An apostrophe in prompt template arguments is parsed as an opening quote. With a template `Question: $ARGUMENTS`, running `/ask why doesn't the user's cache work` sends `Question: why doesnt the users cache work`. With a single apostrophe, everything after it becomes one argument, so `$1`/`$2` are wrong. Any template used with normal English silently sends a different prompt than what was typed.

3. The model gets `Question: why doesnt this work`; with `$1 | $2` the args are `why | doesnt this work`

### Expected behavior

An apostrophe inside a word stays as text, and a quote with no closing match is literal. `"..."` and `'...'` quoting keeps working.

### Version

1.5.0

I'd like to fix this myself: a few lines in `parseCommandArgs` plus a regression test.

issues.title: p2: provider OAuth login fails after a successful browser sign-in when a proxy is configured

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
**What happened?**

In `apps/p2`, OpenAI (Sign in with ChatGPT) and `openai-codex` logins always fail even though the browser step succeeds. p2 installs a plain undici `Agent` as its process-wide dispatcher (`apps/p2/src/runtime/fetch.ts`), so it ignores `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY`. The browser authorizes through the system proxy, the token exchange then leaves the p2 process directly, and the provider's edge rejects it by region:

```
p2's dispatcher    POST https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token (bogus refresh token)
                   -> 403 {"error":{"code":"unsupported_country_region_territory",...}}
through HTTP_PROXY (same body)
                   -> 401 {"error":{"code":"token_expired",...}}   # reached the token endpoint
```

`pi` is unaffected: `packages/coding-agent/src/core/http-dispatcher.ts` installs `EnvHttpProxyAgent`.

This is the same class as #2282 and #11666, but not the same code: the OAuth flow's bare `fetch` is not the only layer here. p2's global dispatcher has no proxy either, so MCP connections, Radius and voice requests bypass the proxy as well.

It is also invisible from the app: `apps/p2/plugins/login/logins.ts` catches the login error and drops it, so the sheet only says "Provider login failed. Check the provider configuration and try again." and nothing is logged. The 403 never surfaces.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. On a network that reaches `auth.openai.com` only through a local proxy (`HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7890` here): `cd apps/p2 && npm run dev`.
2. Open p2, Providers -> OpenAI Codex -> sign in, complete the browser step (it succeeds).
3. p2 reports "Provider login failed".

**Expected behavior**

p2's provider requests and OAuth token exchanges honor `HTTP(S)_PROXY`/`NO_PROXY` like `pi`'s dispatcher does, and a failed login shows the provider's reason instead of a generic message.

**Version**

`apps/p2` @ 2a32a605a (main), Node 26.13.0, Linux, data dir `~/.pi/p2`.

I have the fix working locally: `EnvHttpProxyAgent` in `configureFetch` (keeping the HTTP/1.1 client/pool factories), plus the redacted provider error logged and shown in the sheet, with a test that asserts requests go through a CONNECT proxy. Happy to send a PR if you want it.

This issue text is AI-generated by pi in the reporter's session.

issues.title: Proposal: small primitives for external, terminal-native supervision of Pi (per-tool-call abort, bash-spawn containment hook, progress/watchdog surface, declared-path change records)

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
## Who this is from

An advanced Pi user running Pi headlessly under an external supervisor I
built locally (Pi in `--mode rpc`, a separate Node supervisor process,
systemd user scopes for bash spawns, git-based checkpoints). This is a
proposal for a few small, independently mergeable primitives that would
let external tooling like mine do this job properly. It is not a request
for Pi to grow a built-in supervisor, sandbox, or rewind feature — I know
several of those have been asked and closed before (see "Prior issues"
below), and I have tried to ask only for what is still missing.

Local test environment for everything measured below: Pi 1.5.0
`(local evidence pack available on request)`, Linux, systemd user session,
model `opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash` read back from `get_state`
(not from CLI flags) `(local evidence pack available on request)`.

## Problem

When Pi is driven unattended — long tasks, parallel workers, pipelines —
four failure shapes keep recurring, and today each one forces the external
driver to improvise around Pi rather than work through a documented
surface:

1. **A tool call hangs and nothing outside the process can end just that
   call.** Extensions can observe `tool_execution_start/update/end`, but
   (as #8004 put it) there is no abort handle for a running call and no
   general per-tool-call timeout, so a watchdog can detect but not act.
2. **Bash spawns escape supervision.** A command that backgrounds a child
   (`setsid sleep 25 &`, or a daemon that double-forks) survives both the
   tool timeout and a normal turn end, because nothing owns the whole
   process tree. Process-group kill helps only until `setsid` moves the
   child to a new session (#9460, #10929 are the filed versions of this).
3. **An external supervisor cannot reliably own a turn.** It can count
   `turn_start` events over RPC and send `abort`, but abort semantics
   mid-batch are uneven (#9986: calls after the abort point get no
   result), and until #8432 there was not even a way to recover queued
   steering/follow-up text. A turn cap enforced from outside therefore
   rests on undocumented behaviour.
4. **After the fact, nobody can say exactly what changed.** There is no
   declared-path, hash-verified record of which files a turn touched, so
   checkpoint/rollback and "did the agent write outside its scope?"
   checks are left to each extension to reinvent — and the known
   extension route for checkpoints has real gaps (#8152: cwd-pinned
   snapshots miss out-of-cwd edits).

I am not reporting these as surprises; most are already filed. What I can
add is measurements from running the workaround at scale, which suggest
the missing pieces are small.

## Evidence (local, measured; reports available on request)

E1. **Scope containment for bash spawns works, and process-group thinking
is not enough.** In a 60-minute soak of my local supervisor — 10 parallel
lanes, 3,860 supervisor runs of Pi RPC, 771 deliberate `setsid sleep 25`
escape probes — **zero processes escaped their systemd scope**
`(local evidence pack available on request)`: every probe process still alive at audit time
was inside a live `pi-exec-*.scope` cgroup, read from
`/proc/<pid>/cgroup`, with zero "escaped" and zero "pre-existing"
occurrences in 771 audits `(local evidence pack available on request)`. The supervisor's
turn-end sweep (stop every scope recorded for the turn at settle) fired
in 31 of 3,857 stored runs — the `setsid … &` normal-exit case, where the
bash call has already returned successfully and only a sweep at settle
reclaims the daemon `(local evidence pack available on request)`. Run durations over the
soak: p50 5.1 s / p95 26.4 s / p99 89.7 s / max 122.3 s, 0 runs killed at
the 180 s harness timeout `(local evidence pack available on request)`.

E2. **Per-tool-call caps and a watchdog ladder are enforceable from
outside, given abort + events.** My local six-suite run against the same
supervisor ended `6/6 suites PASS` `(local evidence pack available on request)`:
turn-cap guard 25/25, watchdog 33/33, file-tracking 56/56, integration
46/46 (final run) `(local evidence pack available on request)`. Concrete watchdog rows:
a hung bash call was aborted with a real scope stop (`W1.9 calls=1 …
pi-exec-846716-1bdd90df-0.scope`), a long-but-legitimate call was left
alone (`W2.2 calls=1 tool_elapsed_ms=8024 tool_execution_update=9`), and
the run settled well inside the guard window (`W1.13 settled_at_ms=31335`)
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. The design that passed: the in-process
guard arms the cap and the *external* supervisor aborts only as a backup,
because an unconditional abort at the cap kills the model's own reply
turn `(local evidence pack available on request)`.

E3. **Silent turns are common enough to need a first-class recovery
path.** Of 3,089 normal (non-probe) soak runs, 113 (3.7%) made **no tool
call at all and produced empty final text** over four turns
`(local evidence pack available on request)`; 144 normal runs reached the four-turn cap
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. My supervisor's answer is one re-prompt on an
empty, tool-free settle (`shouldRetry`), never a loop
`(local evidence pack available on request)` — it would be better expressed as a
documented watchdog hook (progress timestamps an external process can
read) than as each driver re-deriving silence from the event stream.

E4. **Round caps already work as an extension; the gap is RPC-side
ownership.** Hands-on, the third-party `pi-turn-limit` extension aborted
a run exactly at `PI_MAX_TURNS=3` (`turn_start=3`, 2 steps done) while an
unlimited control run of the same task took 11 turns / 10 files
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. So the in-process half exists;
what an external supervisor still lacks is a documented guarantee that
its own counting + `abort` behaves the same way (including what happens
to never-started tool calls, #9986).

E5. **Checkpoint/rollback works as an extension; declared-path hashing is
the missing record.** Hands-on, `arpagon/pi-rewind`'s production restore
path returned a damaged file to `version1` and redo restored
`version2-by-pi` on a scratch repo
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. Separately, a tiny local
prototype tracker reported both tool-made and outside-process changes to
declared paths with verified before/after sha256 — but honestly labelled
every row `attribution: "unknown-source"`, because detection without a
Pi-emitted per-tool record cannot attribute a change
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. That attribution record is the
small thing only Pi can provide.

E6. **What did not work, for balance.** An exact-match "reply must equal
DONE" contract failed 586 times in the soak purely because the model
appended extra text after `DONE` `(local evidence pack available on request)` — a
measurement-contract lesson, not a Pi defect, and one reason I am *not*
proposing any built-in "false-done" gate. Cross-process file locking
against a non-cooperating writer, and a true false-done veto, are things
I consider structurally hard and am explicitly not asking for (see
Non-goals).

## Proposal — five small, independently mergeable asks

Each ask is useful alone; none depends on the others landing.

**Ask A — a per-tool-call abort primitive for extensions/RPC drivers.**
Expose the running call's cancellation to code: e.g. the `AbortSignal`
(or toolCallId + a `cancelToolCall(id)`-equivalent) on
`tool_execution_start`, and/or an RPC command with the same effect.
*Relation to prior work:* this is the core of #8004 (closed as not
planned). I am re-raising only the primitive, with E1/E2 as the missing
evidence that external watchdogs are real and bounded — not a built-in
global timeout policy, which can stay extension territory.

**Ask B — documented RPC turn-ownership semantics.** Document (and, where
needed, fix) what an external supervisor may rely on: `turn_start`
counting, `abort` during parallel/sequential tool batches, and an
explicit result for every tool call that was issued but never started
(#9986), plus the already-landed `clear_queue`-before-`abort` ordering
(#8432) written into the RPC docs as the supported Esc-equivalent.

**Ask C — a bash-spawn containment hook, not a sandbox.** A documented
way (BashOperations-level or spawn hook) for an extension/supervisor to
wrap each bash execution in its own named unit — on Linux, a systemd
`--user` scope — and to learn the unit name/pid per `toolCallId`, so the
*external* owner can inspect it, stop it on timeout/abort, and sweep it
at turn end. *Relation to prior work:* Pi's stated position is no
built-in sandbox (README/containerization docs point to Gondolin, Docker,
OpenShell, and the sandbox-runtime example extension); I agree with that
split. #9460/#10929 ask for better killing inside Pi; this ask is the
complementary hook that lets an outside supervisor own the tree,
including `setsid` escapees (E1: 0 escapes in 771 probes when the scope,
not the process group, is the unit).

**Ask D — a progress surface a watchdog can read without scraping
events.** E.g. `get_state` (RPC) exposing last-progress timestamps
(last stream chunk, last `tool_execution_update`, current toolCallId and
its start time). External watchdogs then arm/reset on documented data;
the policy (nudge, abort, retry-once-on-silence per E3) stays outside
Pi. *Relation to prior work:* stream-level silence is covered by #3352
and the merged stream-inactivity watchdog (PR #8593); this is the
tool/turn-level equivalent those do not cover.

**Ask E — a declared-path change record per turn.** For paths declared
to the session (extension- or RPC-supplied), emit/record before- and
after-sha256 (created / modified / deleted) at turn settle, as a
session-visible custom entry or RPC-readable record, with the acting
`toolCallId` where Pi knows it. *Relation to prior work:* #5522/#8152
asked for built-in checkpoints/rewind and were closed with "use an
extension"; E5 shows the extension half works and shows precisely which
record extensions cannot fabricate (attribution). This ask is that
record, not a rewind UI.

## Non-goals

- No built-in supervisor daemon, scheduler, or multi-agent orchestration
  in Pi.
- No in-core sandbox/permissions system (containers/VMs per the existing
  containerization docs remain the answer).
- No built-in checkpoint/rewind UI (extensions own it; Ask E only feeds
  them data).
- No cross-process file-lock *prevention* against non-cooperating
  writers, and no "false-done"/premature-success veto — I do not have an
  honest design for either.
- **No GUI/canvas parity of any kind** — no artboards, design canvas,
  snapshot timelines, or other visual-review surfaces. Those are a
  different product layer and explicitly out of scope here; everything
  proposed is terminal/RPC-native.

## Alternatives considered

- **Pure extensions today:** `pi-turn-limit` (E4) and `pi-rewind` (E5)
  prove caps and checkpoints work in-process. They cannot own process
  trees, survive Pi hanging, or attribute outside-process writes — the
  gaps in Asks A/C/D/E.
- **Container/VM isolation (existing docs):** right for trust boundaries,
  heavier than needed for turn-level taming of a trusted local agent,
  and it does not provide turn caps, watchdogs, or change records.
- **Process-group kill inside the bash tool (#9460's suggestion):**
  worth doing on its own merits, but `setsid` defeats it by design;
  E1's scope results are why I propose the hook instead of relying on it.
- **Doing nothing / every driver scrapes the RPC event stream:** that is
  the status quo my supervisor implements; it works until abort
  accounting (#9986) or queue semantics change under it, which is why
  Ask B is mostly documentation.

## What I have already proved locally (and can share)

An unpublished local prototype, `terminal-supervisor` (Node): a
supervisor spawning Pi `--mode rpc`, counting turns, backing up
an in-process guard's cap, wrapping bash in
`pi-exec-<pid>-<rand>-<n>.scope` systemd user scopes, sweeping scopes at
settle, and recording per-run reports
`(local evidence pack available on request)`. Measured:
6/6 local suites PASS (36/36 + 25/25 + 33/33 + 56/56 + 42/42 + 46/46
checks on the final run) `(local evidence pack available on request)`, and the
3,860-run / 771-probe soak in E1 `(local evidence pack available on request)`. The one real
defect that soak found was in my supervisor, not Pi (a run-directory
`EEXIST` race, 3 in 3,860 runs) `(local evidence pack available on request)` — I mention it
because the numbers above are only as trustworthy as their failure list.
Happy to share the supervisor source, the suite definitions (test IDs
W1–W3, T1–T7, R1–R13, E1–E13, G1, C1–C5 as cited), or the soak data, or
to prototype any single ask above as a PR-sized extension first if that
is the maintainers' preference.

codemode: script repeated an identical tool call 24,018 times; no per-script repetition guard

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
### What happened?

A codemode script repeated an identical tool call 24,018 times in ~35 s (~680 calls/s), each call opening and reading a 28 KB file. Nothing in the sandbox stopped it; the only halt was the wall-clock abort ("Script aborted: This operation was aborted"), which names neither the tool nor the loop. docs/codemode.md documents per-script budgets (max_output_tokens, 16 MB character cap, 100k text()/image()/console calls, 256 MB heap) - none bounds repeated identical tool invocations.

The trigger: an external tool's paging header returned next_offset=<filesize> forever at eof, so the script's exit condition never fired. This differs from #6158 (closed): those loops are model-driven and provider-dependent. A codemode script is deterministic non-LLM code - N consecutive identical (toolName, serialized args) calls is unambiguous machine error, detectable with a string compare.

### Steps to reproduce

In codemode, call any tool in a loop whose exit condition depends on external tool output that never changes (e.g. a paging protocol returning the same next_offset at eof). The script repeats the identical call until the wall-clock abort. Real session: 24,018 identical obs_recall calls at offset=28532 (bytes=0, eof=true each) in 35.4 s; the tool's server-side ledger recorded every call.

### Expected behavior

Abort the script after ~100-200 consecutive identical (tool, args) calls - high enough that legitimate polling loops (same args until a status flips) survive; optionally also require identical/empty results. The error should name the tool, an args preview, the repeat count, and hint at pagination/eof flags.

Happy to implement this myself once the approach is approved.

### Version

1.5.0

labels.name: inprogress
labels.description: Issue is being worked on

issues.body: I was writing an extension that needs to call npm, and on Windows `pi.exec("npm", ["--version"])` just returns exit 1 with an empty stdout. At first I thought it was my own code, but running the same command through the bash tool worked fine, so I narrowed it down to the exec path. My setup is pi 0.99.1 on Windows 11. I looked into the source and `core/exec.ts` line 5 imports spawn directly from `node:child_process` and runs it without a shell — on Windows npm is actually `npm.cmd`, and a bare spawn gets ENOENT, which is an old Node pitfall. I saw that the repo already has `spawnProcess` in `utils/child-process.ts` (cross-spawn) added exactly for this, the bash tool uses it, but the extension exec path was left out. If that's right, switching exec.ts to spawnProcess should fix it. I'm happy to do the fix myself.

issues.title: Support opt-in blocked status for ctx.ui.custom() overlays
issues.body:
👋 Hi folks, first time filing something here as I'm trying out Pi from inside Herdr for the first time and bumped up against this issue pretty quickly. See below! :) 

## What do you want to change?

Let custom overlays use the `blocked` option added for inline components in #11471:

```ts
ctx.ui.custom(factory, {
  overlay: true,
  blocked: { kind: "question", message: "Waiting for user response" },
});
```

Currently, overlays explicitly ignore this option.

## Why?

I'm running Pi 1.5.0 with pi-ask-user 0.17.2 inside Herdr App. A session waiting for an `ask_user` answer still shows as `working`, so I don't get a notification that it needs me.

There are two changes needed: ask-user needs to pass the descriptor, and Pi needs to honour it for overlays. Currently, fixing the extension alone wouldn't help its default overlay mode.

I understand why `custom()` shouldn't automatically mean blocked, since loaders use it too. The existing explicit opt-in seems like the right distinction, regardless of how the component is displayed.

## How?

Track opted-in overlays through Pi's existing status reporter. Clear each overlay's registration when its interaction completes or fails, without clearing other outstanding questions or authentication prompts. Temporarily hiding an unanswered question should leave it blocked.

Would extending the existing option to overlays be an acceptable direction?

issues.title: durable: let a tool mark a durable wait so restarts while waiting don't hit restartLimit

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
### What do you want to change?

Give `ToolExecutionApi` a way to say "this call has reached a durable wait", so its reruns after a restart stop counting toward `restartLimit`. For example, `api.progressed(context)` would clear the task's `restarts`, and its owners' as well, so a codemode call that waits on a nested call is covered.

### Why?

On Cloudflare, a Durable Object whose only pending work is an in-memory await goes to sleep after about 10 s. That await could be an approval or secret prompt waiting on the user. Our 60 s heartbeat alarm then wakes a fresh instance, and `open()` adds a restart to every running task. A `replay: "safe"` tool that just waits again commits nothing. So after 5 wakes, about 5 minutes, the call is parked (1.4) or ended (1.5), even though nothing crashed. Any human-in-the-loop tool that waits longer than about 5 minutes hits this.

### How? (optional)

We patch 1.4.0 locally. `progressed()` goes through the same `#gated` + `commitWith` path as `memo`. It deletes `restarts` on the task, then walks up its owners, stopping at one that is parked or marked for abort. The tool calls it once its request is stored, right before it awaits. I'm happy to send a PR if that's wanted.

issues.title: Groq Qwen3.8 27B fails with HTTP 400 because Pi sends the `developer` role
Let the model drop a junk tool result right after it sees it

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
### What do you want to change?

Let the model replace a tool result it didn't want with a one-line summary, in the same turn it sees it. Something like `prune_tool_result(id, "grep hit target/ build fingerprints, irrelevant")`.

### Why?

I ran a grep that walked into `target/.fingerprint` and got ~40 KB of junk. The model knew right away it was useless, but it stayed in context and was re-sent on every turn after that.

You open a file *because* you don't know what's in it, so you can't predict the output. A human glances and looks away 🙈. A model re-reads it forever.

![Human vs AI: the human looks away from junk output, the AI re-reads it every turn](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/nicezic/69f13fde6fa080a571825b56fd76392d/raw/pruning-demo.gif)

If it's dropped in the same turn, you pay once and the rest of the session stays clean. Only the tail changes, so the cached prefix is kept.

The self-pruning comments in #116 ("pretty good at pruning when asked") are basically this, just without having to ask.

### Everyone wins 🌱

| Who | What they get |
|---|---|
| **Users** | Fewer tokens burned per task |
| **The model** | A clean context, better answers |
| **Providers** | Less KV cache per session, more sessions per GPU |
| **The planet** | Less power, fewer GPUs to build |

Junk is pure overhead: no answer improves because a build-fingerprint dump was re-read many times. Drop it in every harness, and the whole industry does the same work with less. The cheapest watt is the one you never spend.

Filed across 17 agent harnesses; full list: https://gist.github.com/nicezic/69f13fde6fa080a571825b56fd76392d

### How? (optional)

It looks like it fits as an extension: a custom tool plus a `context` handler that swaps the content by tool call id on every request, so the prefix stays byte-stable. The original stays in the session file. Is `context` the right hook for this, or would you approach it differently?

I'm happy to try implementing it if you'd like. To be upfront: I don't know the codebase well and would lean on AI for it, so it may need more review than usual.

*(My idea, written in Korean, translated to English with AI.)*

issues.title: Compaction drops full-output file locators from builtin codemode and bash results

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
### What happened?

Compaction drops the full-output file locator from large builtin `codemode` and `bash` results. Both append the locator after the preview, while `serializeConversation()` keeps only the first 2,000 characters of each tool result and does not include `details.fullOutputPath`.

The saved file and original session history remain intact, but the summarizer cannot retain a locator it never receives. This can make later recovery require searching history or repeating work. I have not measured model behavior or token/latency impact.

### Steps to reproduce

Using the repository's AgentSession harness and faux provider, with no user extensions:

1. Execute this through builtin Code Mode at its default output budget:
   ```js
   text(Array.from({length: 10000}, (_, i) => `${i},invoice-${i},pending,125.50`).join("\n"));
   ```
2. Confirm the result includes `[Full output: ...]` and the file contains all 10,000 rows.
3. Add a short turn, set `compaction.keepRecentTokens: 1` to place the earlier result in the summarized region, call `session.compact()`, and capture the summarization requests.
4. The file path is absent from those requests. Running the equivalent CSV generator through builtin `bash` reproduces the same loss.

| Tool | Saved bytes | Result characters | Locator begins at character | Locator in summary input |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| codemode | 327,779 | 40,278 | 40,171 | no |
| bash | 327,780 | 51,326 | 51,248 | no |

Both executed through real tools and actual compaction; only model responses were replaced by the faux provider. Reproduction test follows in a comment.

### Expected behavior

Preserve the short recovery locator when truncating the preview for summarization, without retaining the full output. Related: #8173 describes a prefix-marker extension workaround; #10452 discusses a broader externalized-output contract. This report concerns the existing builtin tool/compaction interaction.

### Version

1.5.0, upstream base `55a5c6914570e2ae31ca36297654483bbbf46883`; Node 26.0.0, macOS arm64. Test checkout also contains an unrelated `describeTool` patch, which this reproduction does not invoke.

issues.title: openai-completions sends tools: [] when there's tool history in the transcript, LiteLLM/vLLM backends 400 on it

labels.name: untriaged
labels.description: This issue has been auto closed and has not been triaged

issues.body:
Running pi 1.5.0 with a custom provider (`api: "openai-completions"`, baseUrl is a LiteLLM gateway in front of hosted vLLM).

Every request that has no tools but whose transcript contains tool calls/results gets `params.tools = []` in the body, and the gateway rejects it:

```
400: litellm.BadRequestError: Hosted_vllmException -
{"error":{"message":"`tools` must not be an empty array. Either provide at least one
tool or omit the field entirely. (parameter=tools)"...}}
```

This is `packages/ai/src/api/openai-completions.ts`, ~L852 on current main:

```ts
} else if (hasToolHistory(context.messages)) {
    // Anthropic (via LiteLLM/proxy) requires tools param when conversation has tool_calls/tool_results
    params.tools = [];
}
```

Checked directly against the gateway:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `tools: []` | 400, error above |
| field omitted | 200 |
| field omitted, messages carry tool_calls + tool role | 200 |
| non-empty tools | 200 |

So at least for this backend, omitting the field is enough - the empty array is the only failing shape. The `[]` workaround for Anthropic-behind-LiteLLM setups is applied to every openai-completions endpoint unconditionally, and there's currently no way to opt out.

Not proposing a fix - an AI-drafted patch here would be nonsense anyway, and it's a maintainer call what the right approach is.

issues.title: `getContextUsage()` massively overestimates context after retryable network error

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### What happened?

On Pi 0.99.2, a retryable network error caused `getContextUsage()` to jump from about 42k tokens to 330,081 tokens.

Immediately before the spike:

```text
07:53:53  tokens=42707  hostTokens=42707  inMsgs=583 outMsgs=36
```

After a WebSocket/fetch failure:

```text
07:53:55  tokens=330081 hostTokens=330081 inMsgs=583 outMsgs=36
```

The session history shows:

```text
07:53:52 assistant toolUse  usage=33977
07:53:53 assistant error    usage=0
07:53:53 context_edit       replacement=null
07:53:55 assistant error    usage=0
07:53:55 context_edit       replacement=null
```

Pi's retry path creates these `context_edit` entries via `_omitRecoveryAttempt()`. It appears that the later edit invalidates the previous valid usage anchor, causing `estimateProjectedContextTokens()` to fall back to estimating the whole projection.

This looks like the same underlying issue as #10068, and is still reproducible on 0.99.2, which is the reason why I create a new issue. 

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a sufficiently long Pi session.
2. Trigger a retryable transport failure, e.g. a WebSocket/fetch failure.
3. Let Pi automatically retry the failed turn.
4. Observe `getContextUsage()` / the context indicator immediately after the retry omission is recorded.
5. The reported context can jump far above the value reported immediately before the failure, without corresponding new conversation content.


### Expected behavior

Omitting a zero-usage failed retry attempt with `context_edit(replacement=null)` should not cause the previous valid context usage to be replaced by a massive full-projection estimate.

### Version

0.99.2

issues.title: Chosen folder for a moved session is not saved, so every resume asks again
issues.body:
After a session's folder is renamed or moved, startup asks which folder to continue in (`promptForMissingSessionCwd`, main.ts ~697–704) and opens the session there, but never writes the choice back. Every later restart or resume of that session asks the same question again.

Local fix: write the selected cwd into the session file header (atomic temp file + rename) before `SessionManager.open`.

Disclosure: written with an AI assistant from our local patch against v1.3.0; checked against current main.

Published `pi-affix-prompt` (keywords include `pi-package`, has `pi` manifest) — `npm search pi-affix-prompt` returns nothing, so it never appears on the pi.dev/packages gallery (gallery appears to mirror npm search: 49/50 listed packages are found in search results).

Newly published pi-packages appear in npm search (and the gallery) within hours, as they did before Aug 4. The new-package ingestion seems stalled since ~Aug 4 while updates to already-indexed packages still flow.

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): kill whole process trees of bash commands on Windows
prs.body:
## Problem

On Windows the bash and PowerShell tools kill a command with `taskkill /F /T /PID <shell>`. `taskkill /T` finds descendants through their parent pid, so it misses every process whose parent already exited:

```bash
(while true; do echo tick; sleep 0.05; done) & sleep 1; exit 1
```

With `timeout: 3`, the shell exits after 1s, `taskkill` at the deadline finds nothing (the shell pid is gone), and the loop keeps writing to pi's pipes. The tool waits until the output pauses, and the loop keeps running after that. The same happens on abort: aborting `sleep 30 & sleep 30` in Git Bash left two `sleep.exe` running. The #11613 regression test was skipped on Windows for this reason.

Unix has no such gap: the shell runs in its own process group, and `kill(-pgid)` reaches every member, wherever it is in the tree.

## Solution

Windows has no process groups. The equivalent is a job object: a process created inside a job stays in it, and so does every process it starts, even after its parent exits, and none can leave unless the job allows breakaway. Node cannot put a child into a job before it runs, so commands now start through a small helper, `pi-job.exe` (plain C, `kernel32` only, no C runtime, about 6.5 KB):

- `pi-job run <name> <command line>` creates a job named `<name>`, starts the shell suspended, assigns it to the job, resumes it, and exits with the shell's exit code when the shell exits. The command line after the name is passed to `CreateProcessW` exactly as Node quoted it.
- `pi-job terminate <name>` terminates the job. `ProcessTree.kill()` runs it and also kills `pi-job` itself (that covers the moment before the job exists).
- `pi-job hold <handle>` (internal): background processes that are still running when the shell exits keep running, as on Unix. `run` starts a detached holder that keeps the job and its name alive until they exit, so a later abort or timeout can still terminate them. The holder has no stdio (pi's pipes still close when the writers exit), no console, and runs in the system directory.

Failure handling:

- If no job can be created or assigned (for example inside a job that forbids it), `pi-job` runs the command without one, and `kill()` reaches it through `taskkill /T` on `pi-job`.
- pi checks once per process that `pi-job` can run (security software may quarantine or block it) and otherwise spawns commands directly, as before.
- `taskkill` only targets children Node has not seen exit: Windows reuses pids quickly, and a stale pid can name an unrelated process tree.
- The holder runs from a copy in `%TEMP%`, so background processes never keep pi's installation in use.

`spawnProcessTree()` in `utils/shell.ts` wraps both platforms (process group on Unix, job on Windows), and tracked children are now tracked as process trees. If the helper is missing, or the shell path does not exist (so Node's ENOENT spawn error is kept), it falls back to the previous direct spawn plus `taskkill`.

The helper follows the existing pattern of `packages/tui/native/win32`: C source, a `build.mjs` (MSVC via vswhere, or MinGW/clang cross-compilers), and committed x64 and arm64 prebuilds. They ship in the npm package (`files`), are copied next to `pi.exe` by `scripts/build-binaries.sh`, and are required in the source archive. The prebuilds are built with zig 0.17.1 (`zig cc`, the default toolchain of `build.mjs` when zig is available), which links deterministically; the new `Windows process trees` workflow rebuilds them and fails if they differ from the committed bytes. MSVC and MinGW still work.

## Testing

Windows 11 x64, Git Bash:

- New `test/shell-process-tree.test.ts` (all platforms): argument and exit code pass-through (`a b`, `q"uote`, `trailing\`, empty, `%PATH%`), a background process that survives the command's exit and is killed by `kill()` afterwards, and a kill while the command runs. With the helper removed, the background test fails on Windows.
- `11613-bash-timeout-after-shell-exit.test.ts` now runs on Windows and passes.
- `bash-close-hang-windows`, `shell-kill-process-tree`, `6596-taskkill-enoent` pass. The bash-related tests in `tools.test.ts` pass; its 4 remaining Windows failures (plus 2 in `sdk-session-manager.test.ts`) fail identically without this change.
- Bash tool by hand: `sleep 3 & echo started` returns after 210 ms as before, `sleep` keeps running, and the holder exits when it ends. Aborting `sleep 30 & sleep 30` leaves nothing running (before: two `sleep.exe`). Overhead: about 12 ms per command (70 ms vs 58 ms for `true`).
- Linux (WSL): the background survive/kill scenario behaves as before; the Unix path is unchanged.
- `npm run check`: clean apart from `check:install-lock:coding-agent`, which fails on Windows on unmodified `main` too (the generator orders one entry differently).

- New workflow `Windows process trees` runs the process-tree tests on `windows-latest` and `windows-11-arm`; both pass.
- Argument fuzzing: 200 random argument vectors (quotes, backslash runs, tabs, `% ^ & | < >`, newlines, Unicode, empty) give the same argv through `pi-job` as with a direct spawn; stdin piping and a 32,500-character argument work.
- New tests: the holder runs from the temp copy, `run` falls back to no job when the job name is taken, and an unusable helper falls back to direct spawn. Overwriting the installed `pi-job.exe` while a holder runs works.

Windows on ARM: the arm64 prebuild is a native ARM64 executable importing only `kernel32`; the tests pass on the `windows-11-arm` runner. x64 pi under emulation picks the x64 helper by `process.arch`.

## Notes

- When pi itself is killed while a command runs, `pi-job` dies with libuv's own job and the whole job closes, so that command's processes die too. Before, only the shell died.
- `packages/durable/src/env/node.ts` and `packages/mcp/src/transports/stdio.ts` have their own `taskkill /T` copies and are not changed here.

closes #11613

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): edit keeps line endings of untouched lines, diffs only around changes
prs.body:
The edit tool rewrote the line endings of lines it did not touch. It could also fail after the file was already written, for example by running out of memory while diffing a large file. Encoding handling (non-UTF-8, UTF-16) was split out into a separate PR.

## Line endings (#8544)

**Problem.** The edit tool looked for the first line ending in the file, normalized the whole file to LF for matching, and wrote the whole file back with that one ending:

```
a\nb\r\nX = 1\r\n   edit X = 1 -> X = 2   =>  a\nb\nX = 2\n    (both CRLF became LF)
a\r\nb\nc           edit c -> C           =>  a\r\nb\r\nC     (the LF became CRLF)
a\rb\nX = 1\n       edit X = 1 -> X = 2   =>  a\nb\nX = 2\n    (untouched lone CR became LF)
```

**Solution.** Matching still runs on the LF-normalized text, so matching itself is unchanged: exact and fuzzy matching, multiple edits, duplicates, overlaps and error messages. `applyEditsToNormalizedContent` now also returns the replacements it applied. `applyReplacementsToOriginal` maps each replacement back to the original text and splices it in there. Normalizing only shortens CRLF to LF, so the original offset is the normalized offset plus the number of CRLFs before it. A range that covers a normalized LF therefore covers the whole CRLF. Text outside the replaced ranges keeps its bytes.

Line breaks in the new text use the line ending of the line where the replaced range starts. For an unterminated last line, they use the ending of the line before. A lone CR is used only in files with no LF at all (classic Mac files). Elsewhere a lone CR is more likely a control character inside a line.

Fuzzy matches still rewrite the whole lines they touch, as before. They now return those lines as one replacement instead of rebuilding the file, so lines outside the replacement keep their endings.

A kept CR and an LF can meet at a splice seam and would then merge into one CRLF line break. For example, in `a\rb\nc` the edit `b -> \nB` would write `a\r\nB\nc` (normalized `a\nB\nc`) while the diff shows `a\n\nB\nc`. Deleting `b` would write `a\r\nc` while the diff shows `a\n\nc`. Whenever a piece ending in CR is followed by a piece starting with LF, an LF is added at the seam. This turns the CR into a CRLF of its own, so the written file normalizes to exactly the content the diff and patch describe. No kept byte is changed or removed; the one added byte sits where the replaced text was. For a pure deletion between a lone CR and an LF there is no other way to keep both line breaks. Writing the merged bytes and diffing them instead would silently join two lines the model meant to keep apart.

Pure LF and pure CRLF files produce the same output as before. For files without any CR, the normalized result is written directly, as before.

## Diff before writing, only around the changes

**Problem.** `execute` wrote the file and then ran `generateDiffString` and `generateUnifiedPatch`. Each diffs the whole file with jsdiff, which takes roughly 10 to 15 times the file size in memory, however small the change. A two-line edit of a 50 MB file crashed with `--max-old-space-size=256` after the new content was already on disk, and took about 4 s with the default heap. The TUI preview (`computeEditsDiff`) diffed the whole file again.

**Solution.**
- The diff and patch are computed before the file is written, so a failure there leaves the file unchanged.
- The edit tool and the preview use a new internal `generateEditDiff`. The replacement positions are known, so it diffs only a window around each replacement: the replaced lines plus 32 unchanged lines on each side, with overlapping windows merged. jsdiff still does the diffing; the window results are renumbered to file line numbers. The display diff uses the same formatter as `generateDiffString` (extracted into `formatDisplayDiff`), and the patch is jsdiff's `structuredPatch` hunks shifted and written with `formatPatch`, as `createTwoFilesPatch` does.
- `details.diff`, `details.patch` and `firstChangedLine` have the same format and content as before for every file size. The one possible difference: in runs of repeated lines, jsdiff may align a change differently within a window than over the whole file. The patch still applies and describes the same edit.
- The exported `generateDiffString` and `generateUnifiedPatch` are unchanged.
- The model-visible result is unchanged.

## Behavior differences

- Files with mixed line endings or lone CRs keep their bytes outside the edited text. Files that use only CR line endings now get CR in inserted lines; before, the whole file was converted to LF.
- Not changed: matching still builds a few file-sized strings (the normalized text and the fuzzy normalization used to count duplicates), so a very large file can still run out of memory during matching, before anything is written.
- Removed unused internal helpers: `detectLineEnding`, `restoreLineEndings` and `applyReplacementsPreservingUnchangedLines`, which became the private `widenReplacementsToLines`. None of them were exported from the package. `packages/durable` has its own copy and is not changed.

## Testing

- `npm run check`: clean.
- `test/tools.test.ts`, the edit test files, `test/edit-diff-window.test.ts`, `test/file-mutation-queue.test.ts`, the BOM regression and `test/tool-execution-component.test.ts`: 174 passed.
- New tests, all with `Buffer.equals` on the written bytes:
  - mixed endings with LF first and with CRLF first (#8544)
  - lone CR
  - pure CRLF and pure LF with inserted lines (unchanged behavior)
  - multiple edits in a mixed file, each new line getting its line's ending
  - fuzzy match widening in a mixed file
  - diff before write: `generateEditDiff` is mocked to throw, and `writeFile` is never called
  - `test/edit-diff-window.test.ts`: 2000 random edits on files with distinct lines give exactly the whole-file `generateDiffString` and `generateUnifiedPatch` output; 2000 random edits on files of repeated lines give a patch that applies to the old content and yields the new content; a small change in a 20 MB file is diffed in a child process with a 96 MB heap, where the whole-file diff runs out of memory; a replacement of 150,000 lines (no call-stack overflow)
  - seams: insertion after a lone CR, deletion between a lone CR and an LF (written bytes checked, and the patch applied to the old content gives the intended content), and an inserted CR ending before a kept LF
  - random property test: 3000 random mixed `\n`/`\r\n`/`\r` files with random edits, checking that the written content normalized to LF equals the content that was diffed. It fails without the seam rule.
- On `origin/main`, all new tests fail except pure CRLF and pure LF, which pass there because that behavior is unchanged. Without the seam rule, the three seam tests fail.
- Ad-hoc random comparison against `origin/main`'s implementation, 40k random edits:
  - On pure LF and pure CRLF files, the written output and the error messages are identical.
  - On files mixing `\n`, `\r\n` and `\r`, the normalized result is identical.
- Memory and time, 50 MB file with a two-line edit:
  - before, `--max-old-space-size=256`: heap out-of-memory crash with the edit already written; default heap: about 4 s, about 1 GB RSS
  - after, `--max-old-space-size=256`: succeeds in about 0.9 s, about 410 MB RSS, normal 21-line patch; default heap: about 0.9 s, about 490 MB RSS

This PR is AI-generated.

prs.title: fix(ai): defer streamed tool argument parsing until read
prs.body:
fixes #9265

Stops reparsing the full accumulated tool-call json on every delta. Instead moves reparsing into per-access of `.arguments` (cached, so only first access on same version re-parses).

---

It isn't complex code but it's not idiomatic in the codebase and **I'm not sure it's worth it**. It's done this way not to break anyone existing (mostly at least), but maybe making the system explicit in removing this field access and adding getter method instead (to indicate potential ad-hoc work) s.a. `getLastSnapshot()` would be better. (It'll allow cleanup of some copy shenanigans which try to copy objects without triggering field reads. ).

I chose not to do it not to break folks but with AI and changelogs and how pi approaches braking changes maybe it'd be better. Let me know or just change my PR / use it as base for your fix. Whichever works.

---

In any case, this removes unconditional whole-prefix argument parsing from the seven ingestion paths we identified. Reasoning-signature accumulation was already fixed, and plain text/thinking ingestion only appends deltas. It doesn't address frame-encoder catch-up, which can still reparse growing prefixes.

**Do note:** The current TUI still reads arguments on each update, so it can still incur quadratic parsing, this PR just makes it so other more conscious consumers don't have to.

---

 A few visible differences: the proxy now ignores argument deltas after toolcall_end instead of letting alte data override them. Some other malformed event sequences (s.a. pi-messages argument deltas after tool end) can now error where main tolerated them. Live .arguments is also a getter/setter, so strict descriptor-based validators like isJsonValue() can reject it even though normal field access and JSON serialization work.

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): follow local schema refs in tool search and codemode summaries
prs.body:
Fixes #11803.

**Problem**

`tool_search` builds a tool's search text from its parameter schema but never followed `$ref`. MCP servers (Pydantic, FastMCP) often put nested models in `$defs`:

```json
{ "properties": { "options": { "$ref": "#/$defs/options" } },
  "$defs": { "options": { "properties": { "mode": { "description": "reconciliation" } } } } }
```

Search text was `Inspect records options`, so `tool_search("reconciliation")` found nothing. Durable's copy of `tool_search` had the same gap. The codemode `resolves to` summary had the same blind spot for output schemas: a field behind a `$ref` showed as `structuredContent?` with no field names.

**Fix**

- pi-codemode exports its existing local JSON Pointer resolver as `resolveSchemaRef(ref, root)`. A malformed percent escape now resolves to nothing instead of throwing `URIError` (this also affected `schemaToType()`).
- coding-agent and Durable `schemaText()` follow local `$ref`s. Each referenced subschema is read once, so recursive and shared definitions neither loop nor inflate BM25 term counts. Unreferenced `$defs` and remote refs stay out.
- coding-agent `describeFields()`/`describeUnionFields()` resolve `$ref` chains against the output schema root.

**Tests**

- `packages/codemode/test/declarations.test.ts`: escaped, remote, missing, malformed refs.
- `packages/coding-agent/test/tool-search.test.ts`: refs, escaped segments, recursion and shared definitions, unused definitions.
- `packages/coding-agent/test/suite/agent-session-codemode.test.ts`: summary through root, field, const, and union refs.
- `packages/durable/test/tool-search.test.ts`: end-to-end load via a ref'd description; unused definition does not match.

`npm run check` passes.

prs.title: feat: prompt cache warming in p2
prs.body:
## Problem

p2 runs Anthropic (and Claude on Radius) with the 5-minute prompt cache and never refreshes it. Every request after a gap of more than 305 s rewrites the whole prompt. In the p2 sessions of Oct 12 - Nov 5 that happened 789 times and cost about $1,430 extra, 26% of p2's spend. Example: a coordinator waits 11 minutes for subagent reports, then its next request writes 579k tokens again ($2.80).

pi-coding-agent avoids this with its cache warmer: over the same period its idle-gap miss cost was 10% of spend, with 3.6% spent on warming. Replaying pi-coding-agent's policy on p2's request log brings p2's cache read+write spend from $4,674 to about $3,618.

## Change

- **pi-ai**: the warming policy moves out of pi-coding-agent into shared helpers (`src/cache-warming.ts`):
  - `getPromptCacheTtlMs`, `getCacheWarmingDelayMs`, `isCacheWarmingReplayable`, `getCacheWarmingRequestOptions`, `evaluateCacheWarming` and the `CACHE_WARMING_*` constants.
  - pi-coding-agent's `CacheWarmer` uses them, with no behaviour change.
- **pi-durable** (breaking): hooks could not see the exact request, so warming had nothing to repeat.
  - `afterResponse` now takes `GenerationResponse { message, request }`. `request` holds the model, the messages after `beforeRequest`, and the options without the attempt's signal, telemetry and `onPayload`. It is `undefined` for polled deferred responses.
  - `recordUsage` is exported.
- **p2**:
  - New plugin `plugins/cache-warming`: a hook-only Durable extension, with one warming run per conversation.
    - `afterResponse` starts (or replaces) the conversation's run.
    - The refresh resends the request with one output token, no retries and `disableContinuation`.
    - Its usage is added to the conversation's `pi.usage`.
  - Same policy as pi: refresh at 90% of the TTL, up to 60 min while a run streams and 30 min after it settled, and only when the expected savings are at least $0.05.
  - Each refresh asks for the conversation's phase:
    - streaming while `pi.live.run` exists;
    - idle otherwise, but only for top-level conversations (settled subagents and one-shot agents are not warmed);
    - none once the next request would start differently (another model, or a context that no longer starts with the sent messages: reset, compaction), which stops warming.
  - The worker stays alive while a run is armed (new liveness kind `cacheWarming`).
  - New setting `cacheWarming`: `"idle"` (default), `"streaming"`, `"off"`. It switches live through `ExtensionSwitches`.

Radius: the gateway's `/v1/config` already declares `promptCache: { short: 300, long: 3600 }` for Claude 4.8 and 5.x models, so pi-coding-agent and p2 both warm them. Claude 4.5 models on Radius declare none, which is correct: they use budget thinking and cannot be replayed with `maxTokens: 1`.

Not included: a warming status display (pi's `/session` line) and a decision override hook (pi's `cache_warming_decision`).

## Tests

- `npm run check`, `apps/p2` `npm run check`.
- Durable suite (`packages/durable`, all 100 files). The new test covers the request `afterResponse` gets.
- pi-coding-agent cache warming tests.
- `apps/p2/test/p2/cache-warming.test.ts`:
  - Warmer tests on mocked timers with fake models: refresh timing and options, the streaming and idle windows, the cost decision, the stop cases, replacement and close.
  - An end-to-end test in a worker, using the fake provider with a short `promptCache`: refreshes repeat the request exactly and add to `pi.usage`.
- Not run: the full `apps/p2` suite.

prs.title: fix(mcp): close remaining connections when the OAuth callback server closes
prs.body:
After a successful MCP OAuth sign-in, `/mcp login` could stay on "Connecting…" for minutes. `OAuthCallbackServer.close()` awaited `http.Server.close()`, which resolves only after every socket has closed. Browsers may keep an unused connection open to the callback port (a preconnect, or a spare keep-alive socket). Node's idle-connection cleanup doesn't close that socket, and `close()` also stops Node's request timeout checks. So the wait lasted until the browser dropped the socket. `signInMcpServer` awaits this cleanup before reconnecting, and cancellation doesn't apply to it, so Ctrl+C did nothing.

`close()` now calls `server.closeAllConnections()` after starting the shutdown. By the time the server closes, the callback response has already been sent, so dropping the remaining connections is safe.

**Testing**
- Added a test to `packages/mcp/test/oauth.test.ts`: it opens a spare TCP connection to the callback port, completes a callback, and expects `close()` to resolve within 2 s. It fails without the change and passes with it.
- `npm run check` passes. The MCP OAuth tests and the coding-agent MCP tests pass.
- Script reproduction: with a spare connection open, `close()` did not resolve within 400 s before the change, and resolves in about 1 ms after it.

Fixes #11311

Requested by @petrroll

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): read and edit handle UTF-16 and non-UTF-8 files without corrupting them
prs.body:
`read` and `edit` assumed every file is UTF-8. `edit` silently corrupted files that are not UTF-8, and `read` showed UTF-16 files as garbage. This PR adds one shared helper, `src/core/tools/file-encoding.ts`, that both tools use.

## Problem

**Not valid UTF-8 (#10349, #5797).** `edit` decoded the file with `buffer.toString("utf-8")`, so every invalid byte became U+FFFD and was written back as `ef bf bd`. For example, in the Windows-1252 file `caf\xe9\nTIMEOUT = 30\n`, the edit `TIMEOUT = 30 -> 60` turned the untouched `e9` into `ef bf bd`, and the tool reported success. A GBK comment from #10349 (`# 配置：超时时间（秒）`) became `# 锟斤拷...`.

**UTF-16 with BOM.** `read` showed UTF-16 files as NUL-interleaved garbage. A normal `oldText` in `edit` did not match. An `oldText` copied from that garbage, including its NUL characters, did match, and `edit` wrote the file back as UTF-8 with the BOM turned into U+FFFD.

## Solution

`file-encoding.ts`:
- `decodeFile(buffer, path)` is used by `edit` and round-trips exactly:
  - `FF FE` / `FE FF`: UTF-16LE/BE, decoded with Buffer's `utf16le` (byte-swapped for BE), which keeps lone surrogates. A file with such a byte order mark but an odd number of bytes is not valid UTF-16 and is refused: `Could not edit file: <path>. It starts with a UTF-16LE byte order mark but has an odd number of bytes, so it is not valid UTF-16. The file was left unchanged.`
  - Valid UTF-8 (`isUtf8`): exactly as before, `toString("utf-8")` plus `splitBom`.
  - Anything else is `bytes`: decoded as Latin-1, one character per byte, which is lossless.
- `encodeNonUtf8File(encoding, text)` encodes back, with the same BOM for UTF-16.
- `TextFileDecoder` is used by `read`, in both the streaming path (merged in #11750) and the whole-file fallback for custom operations without `createReadStream`. A UTF-16 BOM selects UTF-16 without the mark; characters split across chunks are decoded correctly. Everything else is decoded exactly like `Buffer.toString("utf-8")`, so invalid UTF-8 still shows U+FFFD and a UTF-8 BOM stays as U+FEFF, as on main.

`read.ts` changes only at the decode step (2 lines).

`edit`:
- The file is decoded with `decodeFile` and written back in the same encoding.
- UTF-8 files still go through `EditOperations.writeFile(string)`, unchanged.
- Other files go through a new optional `EditOperations.writeFileBytes(absolutePath, Buffer)`, which the default operations implement. `writeFile` takes a string and cannot reproduce these bytes. Custom operations without `writeFileBytes` get `Could not edit file: <path>. The file is not valid UTF-8|UTF-16LE|UTF-16BE, and the configured edit operations can only write UTF-8 text. The file was left unchanged.`
- For `bytes` files the original encoding is unknown, so an edit is only applied when it can splice exact bytes:
  - **`oldText` and `newText` must be ASCII.** Otherwise the edit is refused. The error says the file is not valid UTF-8 and that only ASCII edits are applied. It suggests anchoring on ASCII text, using bash (`iconv`, or a script that reads and writes the file in its encoding), or `write` if converting the file to UTF-8 is acceptable.
  - **Only exact matches, and only exact duplicates.** Fuzzy matching rewrites the touched lines from NFKC/whitespace-normalized text, which would change non-ASCII bytes in those lines. In Latin-1-decoded text, NFKC turns 0xB2 (`²`) into `2` and 0xBD (`½`) into `1⁄2`. 0xA0 becomes a space and is dropped at line ends, although 0xA0 can be a GBK trail byte. Duplicate counting in these files is exact too: `X = 1` and `X\xa0= 1` are different text there, not two occurrences.
  - **No change within 3 bytes after a non-ASCII byte.** In GBK, Big5 and Shift-JIS the second byte of a character can be ASCII; in GB18030 so can the fourth (U+20000 is `95 32 82 36`). Shift-JIS `表` is `95 5C`, which `read` shows as `\uFFFD\`. An edit is refused if any of the 3 bytes before its first changed position, after the unchanged prefix of `oldText`/`newText`, is non-ASCII.
    - Why this is enough: the edit is ASCII, so every byte between that position and any later changed byte is ASCII. If no non-ASCII byte is within 3 bytes before the first change, none is within 3 bytes before any change. A changed or inserted byte therefore cannot be a trail byte. EUC-JP and EUC-KR trail bytes are never ASCII.
    - Cost: some harmless edits in single-byte encodings are refused. For example, in Latin-1 `caf\xe9=1`, the edit `=1 -> :1` is refused. The error names the alternatives.

Why splice bytes rather than refuse all non-UTF-8 files, or guess the encoding:
- **Refusing every such file** would make the common case need bash: an ASCII change in a Windows-1252 or GBK source file.
- **Guessing the encoding (chardet-style)** is unreliable on short files, as noted in #5797. A wrong guess corrupts the whole file silently.

Splicing bytes needs no guess. Its only failure mode is a refusal with an explanation.

## Dependencies and overlaps

- **#11750 (read streaming)** is merged; this PR is rebased on it and wires `TextFileDecoder` into both read paths. A test reads UTF-16LE/BE through 1-byte and 3-byte streamed chunks and through the fallback path.
- **#11751 (edit line endings)** also changes `edit.ts` and `edit-diff.ts`. This PR keeps main's line-ending code, so whichever merges second rebases. The conflict is in the read, normalize and write lines of `execute` and in `computeEditsDiff`.
- **Line endings depend on #11751.** Here, UTF-16 and `bytes` files keep every byte except line endings. Those still go through main's normalize-and-restore: the whole file is written with its first line ending, so mixed CRLF/LF and lone CRs in untouched lines change, and the patch, built on normalized text, does not show it. #11751 makes untouched line endings survive for every encoding. Whichever of the two PRs merges second adds a combined test: a mixed-ending Latin-1 file and a mixed-ending UTF-16 file, edited with every other byte preserved.

## Behavior differences

- UTF-8 files, with or without BOM: unchanged in `read` and `edit`.
- Files that are not valid UTF-8: `read` is unchanged and still shows U+FFFD. `edit` applies ASCII edits keeping all other bytes except line endings (see #11751). It refuses non-ASCII edits, fuzzy-only matches, and changes within 3 bytes after a non-ASCII byte. Before, it corrupted the file.
- UTF-16 with BOM: `read` shows the decoded text, and `edit` edits it and writes UTF-16 with the same BOM. For an odd-length file, `read` shows the dangling byte as U+FFFD, and `edit` refuses the file.
- UTF-16 without a BOM is not detected. It is usually valid UTF-8 (ASCII plus NULs) and is handled as before.
- Custom `EditOperations` without `writeFileBytes`: non-UTF-8 and UTF-16 files are refused with the error above.
- The model learns that a file is not UTF-8 only through these errors. `read` still shows U+FFFD without a hint.

## Testing

- `npm run check`: clean.
- `test/file-encodings.test.ts` (new), `test/tools.test.ts`, `test/edit-tool-legacy-input.test.ts`, `test/edit-tool-no-full-redraw.test.ts`, `test/suite/regressions/8337-utf8-bom-parsing.test.ts` and `test/read-line-range-display.test.ts`: 127 passed.
- New tests, with byte-level `Buffer.equals` on written files:
  - Latin-1 ASCII edit applied byte-exactly (#10349, #5797)
  - non-ASCII edit refused, checking the full message and that the file is unchanged
  - fuzzy match refused
  - changes within 3 bytes after a non-ASCII byte refused: GB18030 `95 32 82 36` with `2 -> 2X`, and Shift-JIS `95 5C abc` with `\abc -> Xabc` and `\abc -> \Xbc`
  - an ASCII change 3 bytes away from non-ASCII bytes applied
  - Latin-1 `X = 1` next to `X\xa0= 1` not counted as a duplicate
  - UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE files with an odd number of bytes refused, file unchanged
  - UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE round trip with a non-BMP character
  - UTF-8 BOM bytes kept
  - custom operations without `writeFileBytes` give the error and nothing is written
  - `read` decodes UTF-16LE/BE without the mark
  - `read` output for UTF-8, a UTF-8 BOM and invalid UTF-8 equals `toString("utf-8")`
  - `TextFileDecoder` across 3-byte chunks, with a dangling odd byte at the end
- On `origin/main`, 10 of the 13 tests in `file-encodings.test.ts` fail. The UTF-8 BOM, `read` UTF-8 and decoder tests pass there, as expected.

This PR is AI-generated.

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): remove all extension overlays on /reload and session switch
prs.body:
## Problem

`InteractiveMode.resetExtensionUI()` runs on `/reload` and before a session is invalidated (session switch, new session, fork). For overlays it called `this.ui.hideOverlay()` once, which pops only the topmost entry of the TUI overlay stack.

Trace: an extension opens two overlays with `ctx.ui.custom({ overlay: true })`, then the user runs `/reload`. Reset removes the upper overlay; the lower one stays on screen, gets focus back and keeps receiving input, although the extension instance that created it is gone. A hidden overlay (`handle.setHidden(true)`) also stays in the stack and can be shown again by stale code.

Blindly clearing the whole stack is not correct either: pi opens its own overlays (the header logo easter egg in `components/easter-egg-3d.ts`). With the old code, a reset while the easter egg was topmost removed the easter egg and left the extension overlay.

## Fix

`showExtensionCustom` records each overlay it opens in `extensionOverlays` (handle -> removal function). The same function serves `done()` and `resetExtensionUI()`: it hides the overlay, clears its blocked program status (#11851) and disposes its component. Deleting the map entry first makes a second call a no-op, so a late `done()` after reset does not dispose twice. Reset calls it for every recorded overlay, newest first, including hidden ones. Overlays not opened by extensions are left alone. This replaces the separate `blockingOverlaySources` set and reset loop added in #11851.

Pending `ctx.ui.custom()` promises of removed overlays stay unsettled, matching how reset already treats inline dialogs.

## Testing

- New regression test in `test/interactive-mode-status.test.ts`: a pi-internal overlay plus three extension overlays (one hidden), then reset. Checks that the extension overlays are gone and disposed, the internal overlay remains and receives input. Fails without the fix.
- `test/interactive-mode-status.test.ts`, `test/interactive-mode-extension-dialogs.test.ts`, `test/interactive-mode-paste.test.ts`, `test/suite/regressions/5943-session-start-notify.test.ts` pass.
- `npm run check` clean.

prs.title: feat(coding-agent): let ctx.ui.custom() overlays report blocked program status
prs.body:
Closes #11816.

## Problem

`ctx.ui.custom()` accepted `blocked` only for inline components. Overlays ignored it, so an extension question shown as an overlay left pi reporting `working` over OSC 7501. Example: pi-ask-user in its default overlay mode inside Herdr App never shows the session as blocked and never notifies.

## Change

- Each overlay opened with `blocked` registers its own program status source (`extension-overlay:N`) after `showOverlay()` and clears it when the overlay calls `done()`.
- The status stays while the overlay is hidden with `setHidden()` or covered by another overlay: the question is still unanswered.
- Separate sources per overlay, so closing one keeps other open questions, dialogs and login prompts blocked. With several blocking prompts, the most recently shown one supplies `kind` and `message`.
- Overlays without `blocked` (loaders etc.) register nothing and cannot clear another overlay's status.
- `/reload` and session switches drop overlays without calling `done()`; `resetExtensionUI()` now clears their blocked status so pi does not stay blocked.
- Inline components are unchanged: they report the dialog shown in the editor slot, so a non-blocking component shown in its place clears the status until it closes.
- Docs (`docs/tui.md`, `custom()` JSDoc) and changelog updated.

## Testing

- `npm run check`
- `test/interactive-mode-extension-dialogs.test.ts`: new regression test (two blocking overlays, one non-blocking overlay, hide, close in order) and one for clearing the status on reset.

pi-ask-user still needs to pass `blocked` for its overlay prompts.

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): report the real size of an oversized last line in the bash truncation notice
prs.body:
fixes #10015

The partial-line notice in `bash.ts` gets the line size from `OutputAccumulator.getLastLineBytes()`, which returned the live per-line counter. A trailing newline resets that counter to 0, so a 60KB line ending in `\n` was reported as `line is 0B`. The accumulator now also records the size of the line the last newline closed and returns it when no line is open, including lines split across chunks. The notice for the repro in the issue now reads `line is 58.6KB`.

Added `test/output-accumulator-last-line.test.ts`; the trailing-newline cases fail on main with `0` and pass with the fix.

@davidbrai I'm contributing as part of Stanford CS146S. I used Claude Code to help trace the cause and draft the fix; I reproduced the bug and reviewed the change myself.

prs.title: feat: release version tags on pkg.earendil.com
prs.body:
## Problem

`scripts/release.mjs` pushes `Release vX.Y.Z` and `Add [Unreleased] section…` to main in one push, then pushes the tag. CI builds only the pushed head, so the tagged release commit is never built and pkg.earendil.com has no build of a release. Example: for v1.4.0, v1.3.0 and v1.2.0 the tagged commits have Build Binaries and Nix runs, but no CI run.

Internal users want to install a release from pkg.earendil.com as soon as it is tagged, without waiting for the npm release.

## Change

- `ci.yml` also runs for `v*.*.*` tags (the pattern `nix.yml` uses), so the tagged commit is built and packed.
- `preview-packages.yml` also publishes passing CI runs of release tags: `POST /_/releases` keeps the packages for good under the tag (it never moves), then the `latest` ref moves to it. Pre-releases (`v1.2.3-rc.1`) are released without moving `latest`.
- `scripts/preview-packages.mjs publish` decides what a push run publishes (the workflow passes the run's branch and conclusion), reading the GitHub API with `fetch` before anything is uploaded. A tag push's `head_branch` is the tag's name, and a branch or tag can carry its own copy of CI, so:
  - every push run must be for a commit on main, comparing against main's resolved SHA (a bare `main` in compare would resolve to a tag named `main`);
  - a release tag must match `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-[0-9A-Za-z.]+)?$`, have passing CI (CI packs before its tests run), and point at the commit, dereferencing annotated tags, also nested;
  - other names publish nothing.

  This also closes an existing hole: a tag named `main` on an unreviewed commit could move the `main` ref.
- A release happens after the uploads and before moving refs, so `latest` never points at a failed release. The job summary lists the release's install commands.
- A passing push run whose CI artifact expired (3 days) fails with "re-run CI" instead of passing silently, so a release tag cannot go unreleased unnoticed.

## Before / after for a release

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| CI of the tagged commit | none | build, test, pack |
| `pkg.earendil.com/<package>@vX.Y.Z` | 404 | kept for good |
| `…@<release sha>` | 404 | kept for good |
| `…@latest` | none | moves to each release |
| npm, binaries, pi.dev, Nix `stable` | unchanged | unchanged |
| main and PR previews | unchanged | unchanged |

Tag CI runs trigger Publish Model Catalog and Nix, which skip them (`head_branch != main`).

## Before merging

- [x] Deploy pkg.earendil.com with `POST /_/releases` (earendil-pkg `7955990`); until then a tag run fails at the release call and `latest` does not move.

## Recommended (not required by this PR)

Add a ruleset restricting creation, update and deletion of `v*` tags to maintainers / the release process. The checks above already keep unreviewed code out (every push run must be for a commit on main), but anyone with write access can push a `v*` tag on any main commit. On pkg.earendil.com that release is kept for good, takes the version number (the real release then gets `409` there) and moves `latest`, with no approval gate like npm's `npm-publish` environment. Build Binaries (npm) and Nix (`stable`) also act on `v*` tags today.

## Checks

`npm run check`; `node --test scripts/preview-packages.test.mjs` (10 tests, under 2s, against a fake server for pkg.earendil.com and the GitHub API with raw API responses). Each of these mutations fails a test: bare `main` in compare, wrong API field names, no on-main check, no tag target check, one-level tag dereference, `latest` for pre-releases, unanchored or loose tag pattern, no CI conclusion check, dropping `identical`. actionlint reports only the existing `queue:` complaint.

prs.title: fix(coding-agent): cycle to the only model in scope when the active model is outside it
prs.body:
Ctrl+P did nothing when the scope held exactly one model and the active model was a different one. It showed "Only one model in scope" and kept the current model, because `_cycleScopedModel` returned early for any list with one entry. `_cycleAvailableModel` had the same early return, so it also failed when the active model was no longer available and one other model was.

A second bug had the same cause. When the active model was not in the list, the code treated it as if it were at index 0, so cycling forward skipped the first scoped model. With `--models A,B` and another model active, Ctrl+P went to B.

This change adds a small `getNextCycleIndex` helper that both functions now use:
- When the active model is not in the list, cycling forward selects the first entry and cycling backward selects the last.
- It returns `undefined` (the "Only one model…" message) only when the list is empty, or when its single entry is already the active model.

**Testing**
- Added a regression test to `test/suite/agent-session-model-extension.test.ts`. It covers a one-model scope, a repeated cycle once that model is active, and forward and backward cycling into a two-model scope from outside it. The test fails without the change ("expected undefined to be 'faux-2'") and passes with it.
- `npm run check` passes.
- Manual check: `pi --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5 --models anthropic/claude-opus-4-5`, then Ctrl+P.
  - Before: "Only one model in scope".
  - After: "Switched to Claude Opus 4.5".
- With `--models anthropic/claude-opus-4-5,anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5`, Ctrl+P now selects opus instead of haiku.

Fixes #11806

Requested by @davidbrai
