prs.title: fix(onepassword): expire cached secrets on elapsed time
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for this exact head** (`d76c3b49efd`, and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read) as a long-running Gateway, and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD `d76c3b49efd` — GREEN (elapsed clock): the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `d76c3b49efd` (dist built from this commit; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

prs.title: fix: bound Codex catalog startup and client cleanup
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/152886

## What Problem This Solves

Codex catalog startup can load the agent runtime prematurely and retain client work after its owner closes, while competing health refreshes can consume catalog admission during Gateway startup.

## User Impact

Catalog and client work keeps its existing owner, cancellation and cleanup boundaries. A canonically bundled Codex plugin can use the host's state APIs without mislabeling a locally patched archive as an official npm installation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the catalog factory available when the harness loads while deferring heavyweight authentication code and actual client/catalog requests. Close owned transport work, fence native catalog walks, and align the bundled harness with native Codex 0.159.3.

This branch also includes its inherited Gateway health ownership, catalog admission, fleet metadata and serialized build fixes. It contains six commits and 39 changed files relative to the release branch's common ancestor; the final Codex commit changes 24 files. It preserves installed-plugin provenance and the existing local-archive trust refusal. Host bundling uses the canonical package composer.

## Evidence

- 45 focused tests passed on the final source in 27.37 seconds; native version and npm lock checks also passed.
- The canonical Core build completed successfully, with source/dependency and process-closure checks preserved.
- The canonical bundled archive installed into an isolated private prefix. Its content inventory, bundled metadata and native 0.159.3 producer matched the packaged inputs.
- A real installed-loader check passed all three storage cells in 19.91 seconds: honest local archive refused; host bundle opened synchronous and asynchronous keyed stores; host-bundle selection with an unchanged global archive record opened both stores.
- A real isolated installed-CLI model turn passed in 17.05 seconds. It observed the pinned native app-server process and exact response marker, then closed its unit and removed private runtime state. It used a maintenance account, so it does not certify service-account credentials or production review jobs.

The full Core test/check suites and upstream CI have not run for this head. Fresh isolated nine-agent startup qualification is pending. This draft does not claim production release or review-job acceptance.

prs.title: fix(ios): show a recoverable page when the embedded Dashboard gets a Gateway error
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/174955 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes: when the Gateway answers the iOS embedded Dashboard with a plain-text HTTP error (`gateway.controlUi.enabled: false`, or 503 while Control UI assets are being prepared), the Settings tab shows the raw error text, then a false "update the Gateway" banner, and offers no Reload. The sidebar Dashboard pages show the raw text. ## User Impact User impact: on iOS, these Gateway errors now show **Dashboard unavailable** with the HTTP status and **Reload** (plus **Open Gateway**), instead of the raw body and the false banner. Reload loads the Dashboard once the Gateway serves it again. HTML error pages, such as a proxy's sign-in page, still load in the Dashboard as before. ## Why This Change Was Made The iOS Dashboard coordinator had no response policy, so WebKit committed the error body as the document. That document lacks the native-embed marker, so the 5-second compatibility check reported an outdated Gateway. What changes: - The coordinator now cancels a main-frame HTTP error (400 or higher) whose body is not HTML. It records the status in `DashboardEmbedCompatibility`, which already owns the embedded Dashboard's state. - The host replaces the web view with a native page. Reload clears the status and recreates the web view. - Each time the host appears or its Gateway or credential changes, it clears the status, so it loads once, as the web view did before. Switching Gateways rebuilds the host or changes its identity, so the previous Gateway's error does not survive the switch. Reconnecting to the same Gateway also loads once more; a Gateway still answering with the error shows the error page again. - The sidebar Dashboard pages now get their own `DashboardEmbedCompatibility`. Since main passes them **Open Gateway** (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158051), their error page offers it too, and like Settings they show the update banner when the Gateway's Dashboard has no native-embed marker. The Dashboard sends the native status request from its startup on every page, so a current Gateway does not get the banner. - With main's Cloudflare Access admission (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158051), the access check decides each response first: a Cloudflare challenge still retires the session. Only a response it admits can become the error page. - With main's HTTPS Basic proxy credential: when the proxy rejects it and answers the page with a plain-text 401, Settings shows the error page with HTTP 401 and Reload. An HTML 401 page still renders. This ports the macOS fix https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/170361 to iOS. On iOS, the existing navigation-action policy already keeps the main frame on the Gateway's origin, so the response policy does not check the origin again. Overlap: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158051 (Cloudflare Access, now merged) added its own response policy to the same coordinator; this branch merges `main` and keeps one response policy for both. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/172570 (open) shares only the localization catalog and `docs/platforms/ios.md`. ## Evidence Real iPhone SE (3rd generation), iOS 26.7.1, paired over the LAN with a Gateway from this branch running with `gateway.controlUi.enabled: false`. Before is the base `296414b831e` and After is `f0ff7e6c5a4`; both builds ran on the same phone with the same script (launch to Settings, wait 15 s, read the screen). Since `f0ff7e6c5a4` the head adds the reset on a Gateway switch and the tests, and drops a response-side origin check that every response on the phone passed; the 404 and Reload paths are unchanged. `a21e5508a82` was installed for the Gateway switch run below. The current head `39cf8f053b6` merges `main` after https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/158051. In `SettingsHubScreen.swift`, main's Cloudflare Access branches stay inside the error-page `Group` unchanged. `DashboardPageScreen.swift` passes both `embedCompatibility:` and main's `openGateway:`. In `AuthenticatedControlUIWebView.swift`, the error decision runs where main's response policy allows a response. On the phone it was only installed and launched. | Check | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | Settings tab's Dashboard header present (control) | yes | yes | | raw `Not Found` text shown | **yes** | no | | "This Gateway's Dashboard is older than the app; update the Gateway…" banner | **yes** | no | | Reload offered | **no** | yes | Before (left) and After (right): Reload, After only: - With the error page shown, I enabled Control UI in the config (hot reload) and pressed Reload 5 s later. The Gateway was still preparing assets and answered 503, and the app showed "The Gateway returned HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable)." with Reload. - In a second run, pressing Reload 12 s after enabling loaded the Dashboard, and the error page was gone. Gateway switch, head `a21e5508a82` only, in one app session: 1. The Gateway with Control UI disabled showed the error page. 2. I opened **Open Gateway** and switched to a second paired Gateway, whose Settings tab shows the native page. 3. Meanwhile I enabled Control UI on the first Gateway. 4. I switched back and returned to Settings without pressing Reload. The earlier error page was gone and the Dashboard loaded (3 of 3 checks). Checks (iOS Simulator on Codemagic: Xcode 26.6, iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.5) at `a21e5508a82`: - `-only-testing OpenClawTests/SettingsHubTests -only-testing OpenClawTests/OpenClawTypographyTests`: - this branch: 28 passed, 0 failed; - the base with this branch's `SettingsHubTests.swift`: 27 passed, 1 failed (the new test). Its 404 and 503 plain-text cases fail with `Expectation failed: (text.contains(visibleText) → true) == (response.renders → false)`. - The new `SettingsHubTests` test serves 404 and 503 `text/plain` errors, a 404 `text/html` page and a 200 `text/plain` body from the suite's local HTTP fixture to a real `WKWebView`, with the coordinator deciding each response. Only the two plain-text errors must not render. - `SettingsHubDashboardErrorTests` (head only; it uses the new status, so it is not run on the base) checks that a plain-text 404 hands status 404 to the host and that Reload clears it: passed at `88406e8a468`. Since then only the view's reset trigger changed, which this suite does not exercise. - At the merge head `39cf8f053b6` (Codemagic: Xcode 27.1 (27A9275), iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.5), the same three suites passed: 35 passed, 0 failed. These include main's Cloudflare Access tests in `SettingsHubTests` next to this PR's test. | Test | Simulator time | | --- | --- | | `SettingsHubTests`: new test, 4 cases | 5.49 s (5.00 s on the base run) | | `SettingsHubDashboardErrorTests` | 2.54 s | Pull-request CI defers the `ios-build` job (Swift lint and format, unit-test build and run) to later validation tiers, so this PR's CI does not build or run these suites; its `ios-screenshots` job builds the app. There are no CI seconds to report. The times above come from the Codemagic runs. At `39cf8f053b6`, `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` passed. `pnpm check:changed` failed only in steps that don't involve this PR's files: - `changelog attributions`: `CHANGELOG/records/2026.11.1.md` on main. - `typecheck` and `lint`: they ran against an outdated local install; this PR changes no TypeScript. The earlier `ios-screenshots` red ("No available Apple Watch simulators found.", all tests passed) was a runner issue that `main` fixed in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176958, which the merge brings in. prs.title: feat(media): optional silent delivery for audio transcript echo
prs.body:
Closes #187243

## What Problem This Solves

With `tools.media.audio.echoTranscript` enabled, every voice note produces two notifications on Telegram: one for the transcript echo and one for the agent reply that follows, so the confirmation-only echo becomes notification noise.

## User Impact

User impact: operators can set `tools.media.audio.echoSilent: true` to deliver the transcript echo silently (Telegram `disable_notification`: the notification still appears, but without sound) while the agent reply keeps notifying normally. Default is `false`, so existing behavior is unchanged; channels without silent delivery keep sending the echo as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

`sendTranscriptEcho` is the single owner of echo delivery for the media-understanding path, audio preflight, and the plugin-SDK preflight runtime, and it already receives the effective config. It now forwards `silent: true` to the durable outbound send when `echoSilent` is set. The outbound path already carries `silent` end to end (delivery params, durable queue persistence, Telegram adapter mapping to `disable_notification`, the same route `channels.telegram.silentErrorReplies` uses), so no channel code changes are needed. Config schema, field help/label, docs, the generated config-doc baseline hashes, and the common-tier snapshot are updated.

## Evidence

- New integration test in `src/media-understanding/echo-transcript.integration.test.ts` drives the real durable SQLite queue with a fake Telegram outbound adapter: the default echo reaches the adapter without `silent`, and with `echoSilent: true` the adapter receives `silent: true`. Red on base (`upstream/main` f03f131: test fails), green with this change.
- `pnpm test src/media-understanding/echo-transcript.integration.test.ts src/media-understanding/echo-transcript.test.ts src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts src/config/schema.tiers.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/media-understanding-runtime.test.ts src/media-understanding/audio-preflight.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: all passed.
- `pnpm config:docs:gen` / `pnpm config:schema:gen` run; `oxfmt --check` clean on touched files.
- `pnpm check:changed --base upstream/main`: every lane green (typecheck core + core tests, lint core, format, config docs baseline, bundled channel config metadata, plugin boundaries, import cycles, ratchets) except the dead-export scan, which fails only on pre-existing unused exports elsewhere in `src/` on `main`; none are in files touched here and this change adds no exports.
- Live Telegram end-to-end run completed on a real Gateway, as [reported by the PR author](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187312#issuecomment-6527766230): with `tools.media.audio.echoSilent: true`, the transcript echo arrives without sound, while the agent reply notifies normally. No recording or request/output logs are attached for independent verification; a screenshot would not show the difference between a muted and a normal notification. The Telegram `silent` → `disable_notification` mapping itself is existing, covered code.

prs.title: fix(cli): invalidate Gateway-cached MCP runtimes on mcp reload
prs.body:
Closes #164642

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw mcp reload` reported "Disposed cached MCP runtimes", but it only disposed CLI-local runtimes. The Gateway process owns its own cached session MCP runtimes, and the CLI command could not reach across the process boundary — so the Gateway's stdio MCP server kept serving the stale runtime and subsequent agent turns never saw the new MCP config.

## What Changed

- New gateway method `mcp.reloadRuntimes` (`mcp-app` family, `operator.write`): disposes the Gateway-side session MCP runtimes via the existing `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` owner.
- The CLI's `mcp reload` dispatches the method before the local dispose and degrades gracefully when no Gateway is reachable (the CLI-local dispose always runs; the log states which side was disposed).

## Evidence

- Handler regression (`mcp.reload-runtimes.test.ts`): the method disposes all session MCP runtimes and acknowledges `{ ok: true }`. Red on `origin/main` (no such method).
- Suites: recovery 222/222, `session-accessor.readonly` 26/26, `server-startup-post-attach` 115/115; `tsc` core clean in all touched files.
- The reporter's source inspection (CLI-local dispose only) matches the pre-fix behavior; the gateway-side dispose reuses the same owner the server-close path already calls.


## Update — 2026-10-04 (Rev 3 rework)

- **Lease-preserving reload**: the handler now runs the Gateway's own config-reload path (`reloadSessionMcpRuntimes`, the same one the hot-reload flow uses) instead of the shutdown-grade `disposeAllSessionMcpRuntimes` — admitted calls keep their runtimes; only stale ones rebuild on the next turn. The manager's `reloadConfig` propagates per-runtime reload failures (no swallowed errors).
- **Authority revalidation**: the handler reads the request's mutation authority and asserts it current immediately before the reload — a caller revoked during the acquisition wait can no longer trigger it.
- **CLI output**: the failure branch now states which side was disposed and that the Gateway-side reload was **not confirmed** (no more misleading "active agents use new config" assurance when the reload did not run); the no-Gateway case is labeled explicitly. The import-boundary assertion follows.
- Handler tests: reload shape (`reloadPlugins: false`), authority revalidation observed, and the failure path responding with an error shape.

Still open: the authority-chain live evidence (allowed reload, read-only rejection, queued revocation preventing closure, discovery/active-call survival) and the command-scope framing — the reload semantics now match the Gateway's own hot-reload behavior rather than a Gateway-wide teardown.


## Update — 2026-11-06 (Rev 5 findings)

- **Unconfirmed cleanup joined into the reload outcome** (`src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.ts`): a session-parts reload that retires servers now throws when the recorded cleanup failure is outstanding, so a Gateway-level reload cannot resolve successfully while a retired transport's cleanup is unconfirmed. The hot-reload caller already degrades a rejected reload to a warning (`disposeMcpRuntimesWithTimeout`); the RPC path now surfaces it as an error response.
- **Unapplied config reported, not claimed** (`src/gateway/server-methods/mcp-app.ts`, `src/cli/mcp-cli.reload.ts`): the handler response carries `configApplied` next to `reloaded`. With `gateway.reload.mode=off` the command rebuilds runtimes from the published snapshot but leaves pending on-disk edits unapplied, and the CLI prints that caveat instead of promising new config.
- **Discovery order**: `mcp.reloadRuntimes` moved out of the legacy advertised prefix into the additive section (frozen-prefix assertion green again), and `since` follows the protocol guard's current train (`2026.11`).
- **CLI + docs**: the reload command moved to a sibling module (`mcp-cli.reload.ts`) per the line-cap ratchet; `docs/cli/mcp/registry.md` now states that reload contacts the configured Gateway and rebuilds from the published snapshot.
- Regression: `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime-parts.reload-cleanup.test.ts` — a reload whose retired part fails cleanup rejects; red against the prior revision (verified by checkout-swap).

prs.title: fix(workers): verify prepared projects before image capture
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Prepared project images can retain obsolete Git seeds and manifests, and native capture did not consult a project snapshot verification capability before enrollment.

## User Impact

Crabbox verifies the prepared project after runtime preparation and scrubbing, before capture. It preserves current hash memos, removes only obsolete owned project caches, and refuses unexpected namespaces, entries, symlinks or hardlinked manifests before deleting anything. Teardown cannot start a fresh project checkpoint without the provision-owned source-preparation capability. Failures report a bounded check/cache kind with a rebuild action, without paths or verifier output. Ordinary enrolled-workspace inspection remains read-only.

## Why This Change Was Made

Extend existing project preparation and runtime/capture owners with a host-bound snapshot capability, a complete removal plan and fixed-phase provisioning timings. Verification stays inside source preparation and its capture lifetime budget, preserving cancellation and cleanup custody without another capture manager, retained store or schema. The teardown guard is at fresh capture admission, after existing-operation handling, so retained capture recovery/warnings and normal non-project teardown keep their established paths.

This independently reimplements the applicable snapshot pieces of `894d42e54c3` and `5ff0814422c` on main. It does not reintroduce the old Azure SDK snapshot backend, external verifier configuration or image-generation receipt settings. Expanded worker-code verification stays in the separate reuse lane; this PR does not depend on it.

## Evidence

**Real cache-owner proof:** the previously reviewed JSON-only planner fails against the current production memo producer with `unapproved-entry/manifests`. The current planner recognizes both formats and passes the same native shell/Git/filesystem flow. Selected JSON/memo bytes survive; obsolete seeds/manifests/memos are removed. Unknown namespaces, prepared entries, symlinks and hardlinks are rejected before deletion; ordinary inspection stays read-only.

**Teardown capture regression:** independent review found that fencing runtime ownership before source preparation completed could allow teardown to create an unverified checkpoint. Both runtime-grant resolve/reject tests now include teardown and zero-capture assertions. Both fail against the preceding production owner (expected 0 captures, received 1), and pass with the four-line fresh-admission guard. Early-entry guard variants that broke recovery warnings were rejected, not shipped.

**CI fixture repair:** the failing shard expected two manifests but saw one, then expected a manifest-hazard diagnostic but saw `verification/project`. The fixture previously accepted `preparedWorkspace` without establishing that its executable recipe was admitted/completed. It now uses a declarative lifecycle recipe and verifies source, absence of preparation failure and real output before adding hazards; original count/hazard assertions remain. A real owner control with `core.filemode=false` reproduces the former `none` recipe/single manifest and the declarative recipe's two manifests. The exact-runtime old six-test replay passes locally; that replay is not claimed as a fix, and the hosted runner's original executable/index state is unknown. New-head CI must confirm the hosted result.

| Final qualification | Result |
|---|---|
| Complete capture-consumer set, pinned Bun + Node 24 | 225 passed across 11 files |
| Cache/preparation/opaque-Git suites, pinned Bun + Node 24 | 38 passed |
| Explicit Node cache/preparation suites | 34 passed |
| Official core and whole-extensions typechecks | Pass |
| Both changed test owners with normal test-config inheritance | Pass |
| Targeted lint, format and complete diff checks | Pass |
| Test-line ratchet | Pass; slack 10, allocation unchanged |
| Full final-candidate P0–P3 static review with required owner context | No actionable findings |

All execution used isolated task-local state and one Vitest worker. Earlier incomplete-context review attempts were not counted as clean. Dependency containment was reverified across 201 scopes and 5,131 links with zero escapes, including the isolated Node runtime.

Latest-stable `v2026.11.1` preparation-owner output survives current inspection → snapshot verification/cleanup → inspection. This is local stable production-owner compatibility within current transport, not a full installed-release retained-image upgrade. Provider-boundary tests are mocked, distinct from real shell/Git/filesystem qualification. Existing full/runtime builds are retained; this follow-up did not repeat a canonical full build. No paid allocation, native cloud capture, live Gateway/model or live-provider acceptance was performed.

Published CI repair `03dc928ff4a48d72feb7f0e366f2a4cb88875b78` directly extends `1bc0accffa26750b1dfc1e811c8047f8b55c7295`. All 66,746 remote tree entries and all three changed blobs match the tested candidate (`341cf8b5ac014c4eb4fe51917eafc0c9ec0a4ea7`, three files +21/-2); human coauthor credit is preserved. New-head CI is attached and was still running at publication, not yet a required-gate pass. [CI preflight](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42164872059/job/127718882718).

prs.title: fix(codex): cold web-search support verdicts no longer rotate bound threads
prs.body:
Closes #174676

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes: a Codex conversation's native thread is replaced — re-sending its full selected history — on the second turn after a Gateway cold start, because turn 1 recorded the web-search policy from a cold capability probe.

## User Impact
Conversations that start right after a Gateway start keep their native thread and prompt context. A cold "unsupported" capability read no longer forces a full history re-send once the provider's web-search support resolves (the issue measured ~1.2M characters re-injected on a lossless session).

## Why This Change Was Made
A cold app-server can answer `modelProvider/capabilities/read` before its model metadata hydrates, producing a definitive-looking "unsupported" verdict. The lifecycle persisted that verdict's disabled thread config as the binding's authoritative web-search fingerprint, so the first informed turn counted the change as a persistent policy change and rotated the thread.

The preflight now also computes the fingerprint an uninformed ("unknown") plan produces under the same config. When a binding's stored fingerprint equals that uninformed shape and the current plan is informed, the lifecycle adopts the informed fingerprint on the existing thread instead of replacing it. Genuine policy edits (allowed domains, provider opt-outs, persistent denial) move the plan away from the uninformed shape and still rotate as before; a first turn under an "unknown" verdict already keeps a provisional binding and is untouched.

## Evidence
- Regression in `thread-lifecycle-web-search.test-support.ts` (registered from the binding suite): turn 1 under `nativeProviderWebSearchSupport: "unsupported"` persists the disabled fingerprint; turn 2 under `"supported"` keeps `thread-1` with exactly one `thread/start`. Fails on base — the thread is replaced via the "web search config changed" rotation named in the issue — and passes with this change.
- Neighbors stay green: 5/5 `search`-filtered cases in `thread-lifecycle.binding.test.ts` (including the existing unknown-support preservation case) and 8/8 in `thread-lifecycle.assignment-rotation.test.ts`, run with `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on Node 24.19.
- Not run locally: full extension suite and project typecheck (CI covers).

prs.title: fix(ui): stop spinners from keeping WebKit busy every frame
prs.body:
Closes #193929

Related: #151514 (spinner consolidation). This PR does not consolidate spinner styles or change their appearance; it
only moves each spinner's existing mask to a static child.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in WebKit, the Control UI spends extra CPU and GPU-process time on every frame while a spinner is visible. The
trigger is #189847, which draws each spinner through a mask on the same element that rotates.

## User Impact

User impact: in WebKit (measured in Playwright WebKit, headless on a Mac Studio and headed on a MacBook display),
visible spinners no longer keep the GPU process busy every frame. The affected surface is the browser Control UI,
for example the session sidebar in a WebKit browser such as Safari (Safari itself not measured). In the one macOS
app check below, the Dashboard showed no running spinner, so it did not exercise this code; app impact was not
measured. Running sessions, busy buttons,
activity pills and loading states look exactly as they do now. With two running sessions in the sidebar, idle CPU
drops from a median 12.2% to 8.0% of a core in headless WebKit (GPU process 1.9% to 0), and from 30.0% to 20.1% in
headed WebKit on a MacBook display (GPU process 4.2% to 0.5%). #189847 is not in any release yet, so this only
affects builds from `main`. No migration or user action.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each spinner now rotates an unmasked element. Its art is a static `::before` that paints `currentColor` through
the same SVG mask. With the mask on a child that does not move, WebKit's GPU process stops doing per-frame work
(measured below). One shared rule paints the art.
Spinners that used a different mask set `--spinner-art` (default `--spinner-mask`). The activity-pill strip, which
moves its masked frames with `translateY` steps, uses the same split. Pixels are unchanged. The same technique
already serves `chat-processes__spinner` and `subagents-desktop__spinner`, and #128687 used it for shimmers.

<details>
<summary>Root cause, scope, alternatives, risks</summary>

**Root cause.** #189847 (`6feb40ee5b4`) replaced border-drawn spinners with `background: currentColor; mask: <svg>`
on the element that also runs `btn-spinner-spin` (`transform: rotate`). On `6d7347b2da3`:
`ui/src/styles/components.css:356-358` (`.session-glyph__ring`), `:538-545` (`.btn__spinner`), `:3158-3171`
(`.session-run-spinner` and the shared ring animation),
`ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-activity-pills.css:154-163` (`.activity-pill__spinner`) and `:258-268`
(`.activity-pill__atlas`, mask plus `steps(60)` translate). The other spinners follow the same shape. In the
Control UI page, WebKit services these animations with a rendering update per frame. With the mask on the moving
layer, each update also costs GPU-process time (in headless WebKit, GPU-process time is zero with the
old border art, with this fix, and with the rings stopped).

**What I could not isolate.** In a static test page with all 18 spinner variants (including the sidebar's
scroller, transformed window, `clip-path` and isolation ancestors), WebKit animates them with no measurable
WebContent or GPU-process time, masked or not. Only the full Control UI page shows the per-frame cost. The fix
removes the part that depends on the mask. The remaining per-frame cost (below) is pre-existing and separate.

**Scope: every rotating masked spinner in `ui/src`.** `.session-glyph__ring` (bare, artwork, team roster),
`.session-run-spinner` (including the online list's small art), `.btn__spinner` (and `.config-loading__spinner`),
`.activity-pill__spinner` (and its badge size), `.activity-pill__atlas`, `.chat-details-processes__spinner`,
`.chat-details-subagents__spinner`, `.session-worker-stop__spinner`, `.approval-page__spinner`,
`.custodian__history-spinner`, `.device-pair-setup__spinner`, `.desktop-spinner`, `.wizard-sign-in__ring`,
`.wizard-step__spinner`.

Left alone on purpose:
- `chat-processes__spinner` and `subagents-desktop__spinner`: already paint a static `::before`.
- Owner-pair trace (`.session-glyph__trace-run`): animates `stroke-dashoffset` in `steps(60)` over 2 s, a 30 Hz main-thread redraw by design.
- Dictation edge (`.agent-chat__input--dictating::after`): animates a custom property under a static mask, and runs only while dictating.

**Alternatives measured on main's bundle (headless WebKit, single 20 s runs, total / WebContent / GPU):**

| Variant | Result | Why not |
|---|---|---|
| `will-change: transform` on the ring | 9.6 / 5.0 / 1.4 | no change |
| `contain: strict` on the ring | 9.6 / 4.7 / 1.4 | no change |
| `translateZ(0)` base transform | 5.1 / 2.8 / 0 | freezes the ring (rotate 360deg against a translateZ base interpolates to identity) |
| `steps(24)` / `steps(48)` | 7.6 / 4.3 / 0.6, 8.6 / 4.6 / 1.0 | GPU-process time remains, and visibly choppier |
| `steps(12)` | 4.9 / 2.7 / 0.4 | choppy |
| `mask: none` | 6.6 / 3.8 / 0 | wrong art (full disc) |
| back to borders | 8.7 / 5.1 / 0 (median of 3) | reverts #189847's design (round arc ends, one shape everywhere) |
| static masked `::before` (this PR) | 8.0 / 4.8 / 0 (median of 6) | keeps the art and the cost of the border version |

A per-file `::before` (13 copies) was also possible. One shared rule beside `.btn__spinner` and the
`btn-spinner-spin` keyframes keeps the art in one place, matching how the forced-colors spinner list is already
shared in `components.css`.

**Risks.**
- Hosts without positioning gain `position: relative` (containing block for the art). They have no children and
  don't overlap siblings, so layout and stacking are unchanged (pixel diff 0 below).
- None of these hosts had a `::before` before. Hosts without `display` are flex items in every product parent
  (`.btn` is `inline-flex`, `.session-worker-stop__button-state`, `.device-pair-setup__loading`,
  `.wizard-step__progress` and `.desktop-loading` are flex). A bare inline host draws nothing, as it already did on
  main.
- Forced colors: the existing rule sets `color: CanvasText` on the hosts, and the art inherits it through
  `currentColor`.
- Reduced motion: the existing `animation: none` rules target the hosts, and the art has no animation.

**Remaining cost (not changed here).** With the border art from before #189847, two rings still cost about
4 points of a core over rings stopped (8.7% against 4.5%), mostly UI-process commits and WebContent rendering
updates. Released builds have this too. It may be one input to #138918, but it needs its own investigation.

</details>

## Evidence

Acceptance rule, written before the final runs: in every interleaved pair the fix shows less WebKit GPU-process time
than main, the median total is not higher than main, and pixels match main for every spinner.

**Idle CPU, real Control UI page.** Production bundles of main (`6d7347b2da3`) and this head, Playwright WebKit

prs.title: fix: prompt cache misses in group chats when tools.toolsBySender restricts some senders
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/176227

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in a group chat where `tools.toolsBySender` restricts some senders, the system prompt's tool list changes whenever a different member writes. On routes that send the system prompt at the start of every request, such as the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions route used below, the provider prompt cache misses on that turn and the next one. Routes that carry system prompt changes as in-history updates (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/167698) instead append a `System prompt update` message with the other sender's `## Tooling` section on every sender change (read from `session-prompt-state.ts`, not run). https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176167 now pins the tool definitions per session, but the system prompt still follows the sender, and a restricted sender's denied call gets a generic `exec is not available in this turn` refusal.

## User Impact

User impact: group sessions with per-sender restrictions on core tools keep one prompt prefix across senders, so cache reads stay high when members take turns. Permissions do not change: a restricted sender still cannot run a denied tool; the model now gets a refusal that names the sender policy. Restricted senders see the definitions and the system prompt entries of tools they cannot call, the same tradeoff https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175309 made for owner-only tools. Main already sends those definitions to a restricted sender through the pin of https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176167 (Before, req#2: bob's request carries all 13 tools); this PR adds their system prompt entries and the sender-specific refusal.

## Why This Change Was Made

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/175309 set the invariant: within a session, tool definitions and the system prompt depend only on session and config facts, and per-turn authority is checked when a tool runs. Global and per-agent `tools.toolsBySender` is per-turn authority (it follows the sender of each message) but still filtered the tools a turn is assembled from. https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176167 keeps the request's tool block stable by pinning it per session, but the system prompt's `## Tooling` section is still built from the sender-filtered tools. Building `## Tooling` from that pinned list instead would not be enough: the pin exists only in the embedded runner, it starts from the first speaker (a restricted first speaker still costs a miss when an unrestricted sender extends it), and a pinned tool the turn did not build gets the generic refusal.

- The session surface now leaves out the sender policy, as it already leaves out a completion handoff's replayed policy. The turn surface keeps it.
- `resolveTurnToolSurface` gates the calls the sender may not make, with a refusal that names `tools.toolsBySender`.
- On a worker placement, a gated tool now runs at the Gateway, which returns the refusal, so the worker gets no launch authority for it. Before, a gated core tool kept its placement location, and the worker ran its own implementation. Main's completion-handoff gate had the same gap, since a handoff turn already offers the session surface; the same binding covers it.
- Descendant snapshots, cron-creator capture and session-event allowlists still use the sender-filtered turn tools, so children inherit the same restriction as before.

This change is limited to global and per-agent `tools.toolsBySender`. Group-level `channels.<channel>.groups.*.toolsBySender` entries live inside the group policy, whose session surface can be wider than the group default, so they keep filtering.

Codex harness: a sender restriction already turns native tools off for the turn and runs it on a transient thread, decided from the policy pipeline, not the tool list. A gated `exec` definition does not enable the native shell.

## Evidence

After re-ran on 2026-11-06 at `bf21918cf0d` (this branch merged with `upstream/main` `195efadb713`, plus the worker-placement binding) with Node 24.22.1. Before ran on 2026-10-22 against `d238c0e5ce7`; later merges change only this branch, so Before was not repeated.

Real Gateway (each side's build, `openclaw gateway run`, Ubuntu 22.04) with an isolated home and state in a loopback-only network namespace. Faked: a local IRC server with `#team` and two IRC users, and a local OpenAI-compatible provider that records each request body and answers a message containing `RUN_EXEC` with one `exec` tool call. Config: the documented example, `"id:alice!alice@127.0.0.1": {}` and `"*": { deny: [exec, process, write, edit, apply_patch] }`. Messages in one session: alice, bob, alice, bob, alice `RUN_EXEC`, bob `RUN_EXEC`.

Before (`upstream/main` `d238c0e5ce7`): every request carries the same 13 tool definitions (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176167), but on every sender change the system prompt splits at character 22,557 of 55,643. Its `## Tooling` list has 13 entries for alice and 8 for bob. Only 23,065 bytes of the previous request's messages are shared. alice's `exec` runs; bob's returns `exec is not available in this turn. Do not retry exec.`

After (this PR at `bf21918cf0d`): all 8 requests carry the same 14 tools and the same 54,673-character system prompt, and each request's messages extend the previous one. alice's `exec` runs; bob's returns `exec is not allowed for the sender of this message (tools.toolsBySender). Do not retry exec.` Main now offers 14 tools and a different system prompt in this setup; the earlier After runs at `a486c34dc3f` (13 tools, 55,643 characters) and `1e9d792086f` (14 tools, 54,110 characters) gave the same result. This setup has no worker placement; for the worker path, the tests below check that every gated tool runs at the Gateway, and a launch-authority run below shows the worker gets no grant for it.

Observed result: on main each sender change still keeps under 40% of the prefix (the system prompt differs from the tooling section on); with this PR every request extends the previous one. The original run on `847f7fade0d`, before https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176167, also showed the tool list itself changing (14 tools for alice, 9 for bob).

Tests: `agent-tools.prefix-stability.test.ts` gains a `tools.toolsBySender` case (two senders of one group session get identical `{name, description, parameters}`; the denied sender's `write` call returns the gated refusal). Five existing sender-policy assertions changed from "tool absent" to "tool present and gated", including the requester-origin case from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/157806. A before/after test run (base `f7d9d711f86`, head `1e9d792086f`) reports all six fail on the base and pass here, with 96 guard tests passing on both; two of the six fail on the base partly because they import a new test helper, and their assertions fail there as well. Since https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/159863, the `sessions_spawn` description tells a sender-restricted requester that it may start only hidden helpers of the same agent, and spawn admission enforces that. The new case therefore compares every definition except that one description; the docs note it. The shared gated-tool assertion now also checks that a gated tool runs at the Gateway; without the placement binding, four sender cases fail with `expected 'placement' to be 'gateway'`. A launch-authority case in `worker-turn-execution.test.ts` (a restricted sender on a worker placement) also failed without the binding (edit, write, exec, apply_patch and process were granted) and passed with it, as did a completion-handoff variant. Neither is committed: that file is at its 1,000-line cap.

Merge with `upstream/main` `885e57e9f9d`: main renamed `isSchedulerSystemTurn` to `isHostSystemTurn` and now checks a missing turn tool before scheduler reads and owner-only, so the sender refusal sits inside main's missing-turn-tool branch next to the completion-handoff refusal. `scheduled-message-invocation.ts` keeps main's `sessionInheritedToolPolicy` line and the PR's sender-free session scope under one comment. Main removed the `resolveEffectiveToolPolicy` tests from `agent-tools-agent-config.test.ts`, so the sender case there now uses main's helpers. `agent-tools.ts` imports the turn-authority module as a namespace to stay within its 700-line limit. A second merge with `upstream/main` `eb370ce6113` (2026-11-04) had no conflicts; main had grown `agent-tools.ts` to its limit, so `completeTurnTools` now takes the policy filter's arguments, which keeps both calls on one line each. A third merge with `upstream/main` `195efadb713` (2026-11-06) conflicted only where main's https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193098 added `ownerToolCurrentAssertion` to `resolveTurnToolSurface`; both changes are kept, and this branch's patches are unchanged apart from line offsets.

Test lines: the tests add 68 net lines (+112/−44). `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` failed on `1e9d792086f` because main was then over its test-line ceiling and this branch adds lines. Two refusal checks now reuse the shared `expectSenderGated` helper instead of repeating its loop, and `config/test-lines-allocations/tools-by-sender-prefix-stability.txt` allocates exactly the 68 net lines for the regression tests above.

Checks at `bf21918cf0d` (this branch merged with `upstream/main` `195efadb713`, plus the worker-placement binding): `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet --base 195efadb713` passes (6,513,201 lines, ceiling 6,513,230), also with `--no-merge-base` as CI runs it. Every test file that uses the shared gated-tool assertion, plus turn-authority, retained-owner, scheduled-message-invocation, agent-tool-availability and worker-turn-execution, passes: 11 files, 213 tests. A before/after test run (base `195efadb713`) reports the six regression tests fail on the base and pass here, with 96 guard tests passing on both. `pnpm check:changed` passes typecheck, lint, import cycles and the other guards. Its four reds: the line-cap guard's `agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts` at 1,166 counted lines (up 1 from main's 1,165; CI reports it as advisory), a changelog attribution and a dead export in main's files, and formatting of local scratch files outside the commit.

Checks at `1e9d792086f` (pnpm 12.15.0, dependencies installed from the lockfile): the touched tests (times below), `tsgo` on the core project and on every `src` test shard, oxlint and oxfmt on the changed files, and `pnpm check:changed` (typecheck, lint, import cycles and the other guards passed; its three reds are pre-existing and name only files outside this branch's diff). The 37 test files that import a module the merge resolution touched (turn-authority, conversation-capability-profile, session-prompt-state, requester-tool-policy, scheduled-message-invocation, subagent-target-policy and the `agent-tools.*` suites; 449 passed, 6 skipped) ran at `7d8f792ad5b`; the last commit only changes how `agent-tools.ts` imports the turn-authority module and how one test builds its comparison. The docs commit passed the pre-commit hook. The broad suites run in this PR's CI. Since `1e9d792086f` the changes are the `upstream/main` merges, the test tidy-up, the behavior-neutral `completeTurnTools` change and the worker-placement binding.

| Test file | `--maxWorkers=1` wall | CI seconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/agents/agent-tools.prefix-stability.test.ts` | 91.63 s (15 tests) | 3.14 s of test time in `agentic-agents-core-tools` (35 files, Vitest 102.24 s), CI run 39811712060 |
| `src/agents/agent-tools-agent-config.test.ts` | 37.72 s (16 tests) | 8.52 s of test time in `agentic-agents-core-tools` (35 files, Vitest 102.24 s), CI run 39811712060 |
| `src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts` | 107.94 s (46 tests) | 6.08 s of test time in `core-runtime-infra-storage-state-hosted-8` (3 files, Vitest 35.37 s), CI run 39811712060 |
| `src/gateway/worker-environments/worker-tool-authority.test.ts` | 26.20 s (25 tests) | 0.49 s of test time in `agentic-gateway-core-1-hosted-2` (1 file, Vitest 51.19 s), CI run 39811712060 |

Wall times are from `1e9d792086f` on a shared host with a load average of 19 to 31, mostly transform time; at `899e6eb9206` on a quieter host they were 12.30 s, 13.66 s, 14.19 s and 12.77 s. CI seconds come from the CI run on the pre-merge head `899e6eb9206`.

Simplify pass: one decision (`resolveTurnNarrowing`) now names the per-turn policy that narrows the session surface, replacing the inline completion-handoff check in tool assembly; no new state, wrapper or option. Behavior still protected: owner-only gating, completion-handoff gating, scheduler automation reads, and descendant inheritance of sender restrictions. Delta against the merge base: production +50/−17 in 3 files, tests +112/−44 in 5 files, docs +9, one 3-line test-line allocation record.

Not covered: no real provider, so the cache-read percentage itself was not measured; the evidence is the request-prefix comparison. Group-level `toolsBySender` keeps the old behavior (see above), and so do plugin tools a sender entry denies: plugin construction drops them before the session surface is built, so their definitions still change by sender. CLI backends that get Gateway tools through the loopback MCP bridge also keep filtering by sender (`src/gateway/tool-resolution.ts`, the run-bound catalog); this PR leaves that path unchanged. The docs list these cases. Accepted edge case: a sender policy that denies `process` but allows `exec` still changes `exec`'s description and parameters for that sender, because both depend on whether `process` is callable. Likewise, a sender entry that restricts any tool changes the `sessions_spawn` description for that sender (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/159863); in the embedded runner the per-session pin keeps the tool block itself unchanged, and `sessions_spawn` was not offered in the run above. For the Codex harness, owner and restricted-sender turns still use different tool sets by design (native tools on versus off), so this PR does not change Codex cache reuse across those senders.

prs.title: fix(update): recovery guards copy the whole state database on every check
prs.body:
Related: #185656

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: each recovery guard check during an update copies the whole shared state database once the run has its own recovery record.

## User Impact

User impact: updates make 12 fewer whole-database copies, and these guard checks no longer block the update's main thread for the length of a copy. This does not solve #185656's disk writes on its own: most of the bytes an update writes come from other snapshot callers, measured below.

## Why This Change Was Made

Since #188978 the guards in `assertUpdateCommandRecoveryState` and `assertUpdateCommandRecoveryObservation` pass Doctor schema admission, and any read with admission took a private copy, even with `allowNativeRead`. The first read in the same guard already reads the live file natively. These reads now do the same with a fresh reader. Admission and its schema policy are unchanged, and a read inside an artifact-preserving scope still copies.

## Evidence

Native update lanes on Crabbox AWS Linux, base build to the same build relabelled, with a live systemd Gateway and a stand-in writer committing every 2 s until the Gateway stopped. Copies counted with a preload tracer. Disk bytes from `/proc/diskstats` on the root device.

| Lane | Guard copies | `sync` children | Disk written |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base `fc5fec19bde`, 2 GB, `/tmp` tmpfs | 12 | 18 | 51,318 MiB |
| Fix `d8a373bd46d`, 2 GB, `/tmp` tmpfs | 0 | 6 | 51,323 MiB |
| Base `fc5fec19bde`, 400 MB, `/tmp` ext4 | 12 | 18 | 96,873 MiB |
| Fix `d8a373bd46d`, 400 MB, `/tmp` ext4 | 0 | 6 | 90,827 MiB |

All four updates exited 0 and verified the new version. Those heads predate the rebase. The only later source change is the wording of one inline comment.

Regression tests in `src/infra/update-run-recovery-admission.test.ts` fail on base with `prepareSqliteReadOnlyLocationSync` called and pass with the fix. One covers repeated guards, the other a database with the dangling Workshop index, where the source bytes must stay unchanged. 68 tests pass across the admission, recovery and read-snapshot suites. Core typecheck is clean. Autoreview came back scoped-clean and the independent Codex review found nothing.

**Not covered:** the remaining snapshot copies are not changed here. On a 400 MB database with `/tmp` on ext4, whole-database copies written to snapshot staging were about 71 GiB of 90 GiB traced by bpftrace. No macOS or Windows native lane was run.

prs.title: fix(pixverse,kie): video status polls skip the private-network policy without a proxy override
prs.body:
Closes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/179678

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: PixVerse and Kie video task polling does not enforce the resolved private-network restriction when no proxy override is configured. The create request already uses the guarded transport; the status poll took the unguarded path.

## User Impact

User impact: PixVerse and Kie video polling honors the existing private-network policy, including the default denial without a proxy, as Runway, BytePlus, Together, fal, Novita and Z.AI already do. Explicit `request.allowPrivateNetwork: true` and proxy routing behave as before. No configuration change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both polls passed the bare `allowPrivateNetwork` flag. With the flag at `false` and no proxy override or audit context, the shared poll helper had no request options and used the plain fetch. Both now pass `ssrfPolicy: { allowPrivateNetwork }`, the shape https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179321 used for Novita and Z.AI, after https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179245 and https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179273. The provider docs note the policy next to their polling description.

Not covered here: generated-video downloads (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/103083) and OpenRouter or xAI ignoring an explicit opt-in (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/176336, https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/169160) are different stages.

## Evidence

Tested at `3ca1b1ebb60` (base `upstream/main` `951bfb88263`). After merging `upstream/main` `85404c545bf` into the branch, the regression tests were re-run on that base and on the merge head with the same outcome. The merge kept main's restructured PixVerse create path (`postJsonResponse`), so the PixVerse test now mocks `postJsonResponse` like the Kie test; the production change is still the one-line poll option per provider.

Tests: one provider-boundary request-policy test per provider, the same shape as the Novita and Z.AI tests from https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/179321. The real SDK sanitizer, config resolution, poller and network guard run; the API key and create response are synthetic, and global `fetch` is intercepted before the network.

- Policy denied, no proxy: the poll must fail with `SsrFBlockedError` before `fetch`. On the base both cases fail on their assertion (the poll reached the intercepted `fetch`); with this PR they pass.
- Policy allowed: the poll reaches `fetch`. Passes on the base and with this PR.

```text
base 951bfb88263, and again on base 85404c545bf after the merge (condensed test-runner output):
extensions/kie/video-generation-request-policy.test.ts > honors private polling policy without a proxy override (allowed: false)
  AssertionError: expected Error: synthetic poll intercepted before … to match object { name: 'SsrFBlockedError' }
extensions/pixverse/video-generation-request-policy.test.ts > honors private polling policy without a proxy override (allowed: false)
  AssertionError: expected Error: synthetic poll intercepted before … to match object { name: 'SsrFBlockedError' }

this PR: 4 passed
```

Real CLI: `openclaw infer video generate` for `pixverse/v6` and `kie/kling-2.6/text-to-video`, with `novita/wan2.6-t2v` as the control, in an isolated HOME and state directory with the network off and synthetic keys, against a local mock provider. The After ran on a local build of the change before the merge with main (production lines identical to `3ca1b1ebb60`; one test-only line apart); the two production lines are unchanged since.

- Before (base): no guard record appears for the PixVerse or Kie status poll.
- After: the guard fires on the PixVerse and Kie polls (`[security] blocked URL fetch (url-fetch)`) and the command exits 1, the same as Novita on both sides.
- With `request.allowPrivateNetwork: true` on the same build, PixVerse and Kie complete as before.

Checks: `pnpm test extensions/pixverse extensions/kie --maxWorkers=1` (5 files, 40 tests at `3ca1b1ebb60`; 42 at the merge head, after main added 2 PixVerse tests), `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, and `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the changed files.

| Test file | `--maxWorkers=1` wall | CI seconds (at `3ca1b1ebb60`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `extensions/pixverse/video-generation-request-policy.test.ts` | 0.2 s for its 2 tests (the run with both new files took 27.3 s, mostly worker preparation) | 0.53 s for its 2 tests in `checks-node-changed-extensions-config` (the shard ran 5 files in 92.6 s) |
| `extensions/kie/video-generation-request-policy.test.ts` | 0.2 s for its 2 tests | 0.41 s for its 2 tests in the same shard |

Simplify pass: two one-line production changes, no new helper, state or comment. Guarding a bare `false` flag inside the shared poll helper was considered and not taken: it would change every caller of that helper, and the three earlier fixes chose the per-call shape. The existing provider suites mock the shared HTTP layer and cannot observe the guard, so the regression tests live in their own files, as for Novita and Z.AI. Against the merge base: production +2/−2 lines, tests +98, docs +4/−2. Test-line budget: `config/test-lines-allocations/video-poll-ssrf-policy.txt` allocates these 98 net test lines, because the regressions must run the real guarded poll that the existing Kie and PixVerse suites mock out; `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet --base 85404c545bf` passes.

Other pollers checked: every other video provider's status poll already goes through the guard (fixed upstream, or guarded through an audit context or its own guarded fetch). DeepInfra and Vydra pass a bare flag too, but always set an audit context.

Not covered: no real PixVerse or Kie account; the provider was a local mock.

Closes #193947

**Draft — live Telegram Test Server validation is still required.**

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Telegram media callback cards disappearing (or losing their buttons) when the attempted replacement text message fails to send.

## User Impact

A failed replacement no longer destroys the original interactive card. Successful replacement still retires the old card, including clearing stale buttons when deletion fails. No configuration changes or user actions are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing callback recovery deleted the media message before attempting its replacement. Send the replacement first, then perform the existing best-effort cleanup. This is a one-line net production change using the existing owner, with no new helper, state, API, or dependencies.

## Evidence

- Base: `eb77d91994befa7194122199a963d75087b7739e`; candidate: `4985658b3e1f135bec67fd805db3c62559f26f11`.
- Red on unchanged base production code: the real grammY HTTP transport regression produced `editMessageText -> deleteBusinessMessages -> sendMessage`, including when the replacement `sendMessage` was rejected. Both new expectations failed for that ordering; five existing controls passed.

The existing router integration proves successful replacement followed by failed deletion still clears stale buttons. Transport tests preserve business/topic payload checks and prove rejected replacement causes no destructive cleanup.
- Source-aware scoped TypeScript check using the repository extension-test compiler configuration and the three touched files: passed. Source-aware typed lint through `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`: 0 warnings/errors across three files, 293 rules. Format, `git diff --check`, and line-cap ratchet passed.
- Shared autoreview, complete local change against the pinned base, P0–P3: scoped-clean, no findings. The reviewer did not execute tests and noted limited unchanged context. The implementer ran the tests above separately.

prs.title: test(ui): wait for Chromium to blur a disabled field before reading it
prs.body:
Unblocks #193943 and any other PR whose `checks-ui` shard runs this file.

## What Problem This Solves

`ui/src/components/form-controls.browser.test.ts` fails intermittently on main. The failing case is "preserves shared field states and forced-colors focus indicators", at the `<field|usage|agent> disabled while hovered` assertion. It failed in 4 of 5 local runs on current main, on a different control each time, and it fails the `checks-ui (2/3)` shard on unrelated PRs.

## Why This Change Was Made

#193468 added that assertion. It sets `disabled` on the focused control, then reads the computed style right away. Chromium removes focus from a newly disabled element at its next rendering update, not immediately, so the read often still sees the keyboard-focus border (`rgb(86, 120, 154)`) instead of the resting border.

The test now polls until the style settles. Product styles are unchanged: once Chromium has removed focus, the disabled control shows the resting border, opacity 0.5 and the not-allowed cursor, as the test expects.

## Evidence

- On current main: 4 of 5 runs fail (`usage`, `agent`, `agent`, `usage`).
- With this change: 8 of 8 runs pass.
- Autoreview (Claude engine): no findings.
