prs.title: fix(runtime): reject tool-call envelopes leaked into prose instead of rendering them
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (head `87432f7ae2`; merges cleanly with current master `0f8fb9d372`)
- **What changed and why:**
  - **Symptom.** On `gpt-5.6` via the codex provider (intermittent, about three occurrences in one evening on a production instance), a turn's tool calls arrived glued **into** the visible reply as raw JSON instead of the structured channel: prose, then `{"content":null,"tool_calls":[…]}` followed by a Gemini-style `{"content":…,"tool_code":…,"tool_name":…}` stub, then more prose and a hallucinated success claim. The user saw envelope bytes as garbage text, the tool never executed, and the model then claimed the work was done.
  - **Why every existing layer missed it.** The response starts with prose, so the whole-response JSON pass and every envelope classifier — all gated on the text *starting* with `{`/`[`/tag/fence — never fire. The field payload was additionally malformed by a python-style `\'` escape inside the `arguments` string: invalid JSON, plausibly why the provider delivered the calls as text in the first place.
  - **Fix: detect and retry, never execute.** A complete tool protocol object naming an active tool — after prose, inside other JSON, or inside malformed outer text — now trips the parse-issue path in `detect_tool_call_parse_issue_for_known_tools`, so the turn is rejected and retried with model feedback instead of rendered. Detection scans for JSON values, walks each parsed value's whole tree, and covers canonical, alias- and Responses-shaped envelopes, malformed protocol members of a complete envelope, and python tool stubs. A `\'`-repaired copy is scanned (removed only at odd backslash-run parity, so the legal `\\'` is untouched), so the observed malformed payload is still seen. Every leak-detection site that decides whether a name in model output refers to an active tool applies the parser's alias normalization, so a leak naming `bash` is treated like one naming `shell`. The detector is deliberately bounded to these shapes; what it does not cover is listed under Security.
  - **Why not execute the leaked call.** An earlier revision of this PR salvaged calls from prose. Review showed, and three further review passes on progressively stricter scanners confirmed, that whether an embedded object is a genuine leak or data the model is quoting (a JSON array, a truncated transcript tail, a YAML-style mapping) cannot be decided from text. Executing it therefore lets model-echoed business data smuggle a tool invocation. Rejection with retry fixes the user-visible defect — no protocol bytes rendered, no false completion — while the model re-issues the call through the structured channel.
  - **Streaming parity.** Final rejection cannot retract text already streamed, so the stream guard reaches the completed-response verdict from the same inputs. It holds an unfinished JSON-like value from its own opener, so a leak split across deltas is not forwarded before an identifying key arrives, while ordinary inline JSON in prose keeps streaming; brackets inside strings do not count, and the per-chunk scan is bounded by bytes examined so a run of closed values cannot crowd out a later unfinished candidate. It receives the active tool names from the turn's own tool specs, independently of whether the provider request carries native tool specs, so the text-tool route is covered. It checks the whole buffer on every release, because a release emits everything ahead of the candidate anchor too.
  - **Documentation guard.** A reply that quotes the protocol while explaining it is not rejected, on the completed and the streaming path. Two questions are answered separately. `looks_like_tool_protocol_example` decides whether the reply is documentation; for tag- and fence-delimited calls that is judged for the reply as a whole by any example or sample wording in its visible text ("Sample tool call:", "Example tool call:", "示例如下:", or an explicit framing phrase), because tags are an executable format and a tag that is not documentation is parsed as a real call. `unframed_embedded_protocol_mentions_known_tool` then rejects a reply that is documentation as a whole but carries a bare protocol object naming an active tool without its own framing clause, so one illustrated example exempts only itself. Framing is explicit illustrative phrasing in the clause that ends at the object: only prose counts, so quoted data cannot frame the leak after it; a sentence terminator or a line break closes the clause, with a fence opener excepted and the periods of "e.g." not counted; and a stray tag marker without its own closer is not a span that can hide a leak. Ordinary narration words ("creating the sample page", `examples/`, documentation-domain links) never qualify.
- **Scope boundary:** No text-embedded envelope is ever parsed into a call. No change to the structured tool-call channel, to any provider's request/response mapping, to the whole-response parse passes, to retry policy, or to tool approval. Only the observed `\'` defect is repaired; other malformations are not. The provider-side root cause is not addressed.
- **Blast radius:** The runtime's known-tool parse-issue detection (every provider's text path), the streaming protocol hold-back, and the channel orchestrator's stripping of isolated tool-call artifacts, which now recognizes aliased tool names as its envelope branch already did. A false positive rejects and retries a reply that quotes a complete protocol object naming an active tool without framing it (see Security). A shape outside the detector's scope is rendered as text.
- **Linked issue(s):** No tracking issue was filed; the defect was diagnosed directly from production payloads. Related #10445 (landed; this branch was rebased onto it at the reviewer's request).
- **Labels:** `bug`, `agent`, `channel`, `runtime`, `experienced contributor`, `channel:core`, `domain:security`, `risk:high`, `size:XL`, `topic:provider-transport`

### What this does, simply

Sometimes a model answers in words but also pastes a tool call into the text, as raw JSON, instead of sending it through the proper channel. Before this change, that pasted text was shown to the user as if it were part of the answer, and in one version of this fix it was even run. Now the runtime notices a complete tool call hiding in the text, refuses the whole reply, and asks the model again, so the user never sees protocol bytes and nothing pasted into prose is ever executed. The streaming path holds back the same text before it reaches the screen, since a rejection cannot take back what was already shown. A reply that merely explains or quotes the format as an example ("for example, a call looks like this: …", in English, Spanish, French, Japanese or Chinese) is left alone.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — the leak is intermittent and provider-side, so a live A/B cannot be reproduced on demand; the byte-exact field payloads are replayed deterministically in the regression suite instead.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required workspace build/clippy/test matrix covers the three changed crates; the change is Rust-only with no visual surface. At head `87432f7ae2` (run 38075876268) the [CI Required Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114284927332) passes, with [Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600299), [Lint](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600273) including the rustdoc gate, [Security](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282600005) and [Parallel Runtime Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38075876268/job/114282696530) green; 48 jobs succeeded and none failed.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None for the detection boundary — every placement and guard rule is pinned by a deterministic regression. Documented detection gaps are listed under Security.
- **Commands run and tail output (at head `87432f7ae2`; exit codes captured from cargo itself):**

```text
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                        # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings   # clean
$ RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels   # clean
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: ok. 224 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored      (zeroclaw-tool-call-parser)
test result: ok. 5644 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored     (zeroclaw-runtime)
$ bash scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh    # defaults, 3 runs x 16 threads: runtime 5644 and channels 1972 on every run
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh          # passed
```
The same gates pass on the merge result with current `master` (`0f8fb9d372`).

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Both byte-exact field payloads are detected and produce no call; the first is left untouched as visible text for the runtime to reject. At the stream boundary: a python-stub leak split at every byte boundary is never forwarded; the text-tool route suppresses it with no native tool specs; an example framed in an earlier delta streams unchanged, and a framed stub split at every byte still streams whole, while an unrelated earlier phrase exempts nothing; a framed illustration followed by an unframed leak, in one delta or several, suppresses the leak, as does a tag example followed by a bare leak; a unicode-escaped key or a named tool-result envelope ahead of the candidate anchor is not released; and inline JSON in prose keeps streaming. Parser regressions cover every placement surfaced across the reviews — the reviewer's prose-prefixed business array, array-wrapped leaks, complete envelopes inside valid, truncated or malformed outer arrays and objects, closers hidden in double- and single-quoted strings, apostrophes and inch marks, repaired `\'` escapes, tag-adjacent and `<think>`-wrapped structure, a quoted transcript tail, a tuple, and plain narration — each asserting no call, detection, and that the documentation guard stays off; alias names on the stub, tag and malformed-text arms; quoted data that tries to frame a following leak; a line break closing the framing clause; "e.g." framing only its own clause, while "i.e." and a snake_case `page_g_2` frame nothing; stray and plural tag markers that must not hide a leak; a tag or fenced example beside a separate unframed leak; and genuine documentation, including a second framed example, that stays exempt. At the runtime boundary: leaked envelopes and stubs are rejected with no tool call; a tag example beside a bare leak is rejected without its tag executing; five ordinary tag-documentation replies (period-ended lead-in, a dotted file name, a transcript, a numbered list, a trailing explanation after a fence) render with no call; and five ordinary replies (an API explanation quoting a tool result, a Python code sample, an elided example, markdown-link prose, a framed envelope) render without a retry. Every mechanism was mutation-checked: reverting it fails a dedicated regression. Two named exceptions: the stream guard applies the unframed check at both the candidate and the release site, and each alone is backstopped by the other, so only removing both fails the streaming regression; and the candidate-level framing check is backstopped by the whole-buffer release check. NOT verified: a live provider reproduction (intermittent).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no interface presentation changed; leaked protocol bytes are no longer rendered.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `87432f7ae2`; no interface surface. Evidence is the exact-head CI above and the deterministic stream-guard, parser and runtime-boundary regressions.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** A reply embedding an unframed complete protocol object for an active tool is suppressed from the stream and rejected for retry; a reply that frames it as an explicit example is streamed and rendered unchanged, and a documented tag call is rendered, not executed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full-workspace clippy/test left to CI; the scoped runs and CI's parallel runtime gate above cover the three changed crates.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No — fixtures reproduce the leak's structure with illustrative command strings and no personal data.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes**
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: this changes how untrusted model output that embeds tool protocol JSON is handled — it is rejected and retried instead of rendered. Nothing embedded in text is ever executed, so model-echoed data cannot trigger a tool. Residual risks: (1) a reply that quotes a complete protocol object naming an active tool without an explicit example phrase in its own clause is rejected, and if the model keeps quoting it the retries end in the existing fallback error; (2) the detector is bounded, and these are not detected, so such replies are rendered as text: an object that is itself cut off and never closes, replies longer than the 64 KiB scan bound, a tool result that names no tool, a bare call object with no container key (the channel orchestrator strips it only when it stands alone on a line outside a code fence), a duplicate or whitespace-padded protocol key, and a tag leak in a reply whose visible text uses example or sample wording, which is rendered as text rather than executed.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: N/A

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` of the branch commit. The change is stateless — no schema, config, or persisted data — so a revert fully restores prior behavior on the next build.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** false-positive rejections appear as turns retried with the "response resembled an internal tool protocol envelope but no valid tool call could be parsed" feedback on replies that only quoted protocol data, and in the worst case the fallback error after retries; a detection regression shows known-tool protocol JSON rendered to users again.

prs.title: feat(runtime): pre-turn tool-elicitation hints behind default-off flag (#7431, 2/2)
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Second and final slice of the accepted #7431 v1 design, consuming the trigger contract that #9766 landed. When the new per-agent runtime-profile flag `tool_elicitation` is on (default off, fail closed when config or agent alias is absent) and the turn is `TurnOrigin::Channel`, the elicitation decision is made once per logical turn at the dispatch edge: the channel orchestrator captures the inbound message content at queue ingress — `PendingTurn.inbound_content`, beside the existing immutable `delivery_message_id`, refreshed only by the debouncer's merge of the user's own consecutive messages — before the modifying `on_message_received` hook (which current master runs in the dispatch path ahead of conversation-lane admission), thinking-directive stripping, media transcription, link enrichment, the channel preamble, and any memory enrichment, carries it through the lane to the turn, and prescans that immutable snapshot against callable tools' `invocation_triggers()` (static registry plus the activated deferred set). Exclusions use one shared predicate (trimmed, case-insensitive) across elicitation, advertisement, and execution, and the prescan scans under the turn's own exclusion list (`per_turn_excluded_tools`, the same binding execution uses) rather than a second derivation of it. The decision, hit or no-match, is recorded in runtime-owned per-turn state; the engine only consumes that record — it never scans provider-visible or pipeline-generated text — injecting the one-line hint on a recorded hit.
  - On a hit, a one-line hint naming the matched tool rides the latest user message's content — the same idiom as memory-context injection, because a separate system message gets hoisted to context start by provider-side normalization, exactly the weak position the accepted design rejects. Longest trigger wins; excluded tools are skipped; an idempotence guard keeps a model-switch retry from stacking the hint.
  - Telemetry records tool names only, never message text: `prefilter_hit`, `hint_injected`, and `tool_called_after_hint` (at most once per turn, when the hinted tool actually executes), all correlated by trace id. This is the evidence base the accepted plan requires before any v2 extraction discussion.
  - The orchestrator captures and scans original inbound text. The engine consumes the decision, injects the hint beside memory-context injection, and observes tool execution for correlation telemetry.
- **Scope boundary:** No extraction call, no `HookRunner::run_before_llm_call` wake, no new routing writer — `send_via` remains the only routing writer and the prefilter never executes a tool. The hint nudges; the model stays the decision-maker.
- **Blast radius:** Channel orchestration, the runtime tool loop and advertisement, activated-tool snapshots, and the runtime-profile schema. With the flag off, no elicitation decision or hint is produced; the remaining flag-independent cost is one copy of each inbound message's text carried with its pending turn (the hint-state map is never created and never locked unless some agent records a decision). Advertisement also adopts execution's existing trimmed, case-insensitive exclusions, independently of the flag.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #7431 (the issue stays open to evaluate the telemetry and make the v2 decision). Related #9766 (slice 1), #7361 (`send_via` contract), #8619 (the injection seam this sits beside). The bounded placement exception was approved and landed in #11047.
- **Labels:** `enhancement`, `agent`, `channel`, `config`, `runtime`, `tool`, `experienced contributor`, `channel:core`, `tool:mcp`, `follow-up`, `risk:medium`, `size:XL`

### What this does, simply

Some messages clearly ask for a specific tool, like "send this to my email", but the model sometimes just replies in text instead. With this opt-in setting turned on for an agent, ZeroClaw checks the user's own message for phrases that tools have registered. If one matches, it adds a short note telling the model that tool may be relevant. The model still decides, and nothing runs automatically. With the setting off, which is the default, nothing changes.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` (any messaging channel; gating is on `TurnOrigin::Channel`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** an agent with a runtime profile setting `tool_elicitation = true` and a tool exposing `invocation_triggers()` (e.g. `send_via` from #9766); a second agent left on a default profile as control
- **Steps to run:** send the flagged agent a channel message containing a trigger phrase (e.g. "send this to my email"), then a neutral message ("what's the weather"); watch logs
- **Expected on this branch (after):** `prefilter_hit` + `hint_injected` events (tool name + trace id only) for the trigger message; the model retains the choice to invoke `send_via`, and `tool_called_after_hint` is emitted if it does. No elicitation events or hint should appear for the neutral message or the control agent. A representative real-provider path has been exercised; general invocation reliability remains unmeasured.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** no events, and the model routes by prose luck — the trigger phrase produces an ordinary text reply on channels where it should invoke `send_via`

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required workspace build/clippy/test matrix covers the changed Rust crates; no visual surface changed.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None for the input boundary at head `c158553d4d`: end-to-end pipeline regressions (the real `run_message_dispatch_loop`, so the modifying hook runs where production runs it, with a recording provider) prove that hook-spliced enrichment containing a genuine trigger produces no hint while the same pipeline still hints on a genuine inbound trigger; engine-level regressions cover generated channel context (binding no-match), enriched-history model-switch retries, and exclusion case/whitespace normalization across scan, advertisement, and execution. The [webhook/Gemini smoke](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/10325#issuecomment-5635357583), run at `f613e1432c`, demonstrates the flag-off control and enabled hint-to-call path. Head `c158553d4d` is a fresh merge of current `master` (`74362c2d6b`) plus the review changes; the earlier required-CI pass and both approvals are on pre-refresh heads, so this head needs fresh required CI and re-review.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
# Local validation at head c158553d4d (merge of master 74362c2d6b + review changes)
$ cargo check --tests -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels   # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings   # exit 0
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib tool_elicitation
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: ok. 5464 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored   # elicitation suite 28
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib
test result: ok. 1969 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored   # incl. both pipeline-boundary regressions via the dispatch loop
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh && cargo fmt --all -- --check   # passed / clean

# Earlier local validation at head c1623136a1 (previous master merge)
$ cargo check --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets   # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-gateway --tests   # no warnings
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: ok. 4459 passed; 0 failed; 6 ignored
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib
test result: ok. 1735 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored   # incl. both pipeline-boundary regressions via the dispatch loop
$ bash scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh   # defaults, 3 runs x 16 threads: runtime 4459 and channels 1735 on every run
$ bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh && cargo fmt --all -- --check   # passed / clean

# Local validation at head f613e1432c (pipeline-boundary snapshot + shared advertisement exclusions)
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- --test-threads=16
test result: ok. 4264 passed; 0 failed; 5 ignored   # elicitation suite 28, tool_specs 18
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib
test result: ok. 1550 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored   # incl. the 2 end-to-end pipeline-boundary regressions

# Historical local validation at head 2311e3d612
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check          # clean
$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-tools -p zeroclaw-config --tests   # no warnings
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib elicitation
test result: ok. 26 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- --test-threads=16
test result: ok. 3875 passed; 0 failed; 3 ignored   # telemetry regression also repeated 3x under 16 threads, green
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib tool_elicitation
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** At `f613e1432c`, an isolated aarch64 daemon with Gemini 2.5 Flash received real HMAC webhook messages. With the flag unset, no elicitation events appeared. With it enabled, a trigger produced a hint; a fresh-session request to an existing webhook target produced one correlated `send_via` invocation event with the same trace ID. See the [smoke report](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/10325#issuecomment-5635357583). This is representative integration evidence, not a measured model-reliability improvement. The smoke predates the `c1623136a1` master merge, which moved only the snapshot's capture point (the hook now runs in the dispatch path), and the `c158553d4d` refresh, where master's agent-lifecycle turn lease now hands the pending turn to `run_conversation_turn` whole; the snapshot rides inside it unchanged, from queue ingress through the debouncer's merge to the prescan. That boundary is covered deterministically by the dispatch-loop regressions, and the negative one was mutation-checked — pointing the prescan at post-hook `msg.content` makes it fail. Deterministic tests cover generated-context immunity, retry state, exclusions, lifecycle cleanup, and invocation-only telemetry.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no user-visible interface state changed. The hint is model-visible request text; it is never part of a rendered interface surface.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** N/A — there is no interface output to capture. Behavioral evidence for the changed surface is the deterministic dispatch-loop regressions at head `c158553d4d` and the linked webhook smoke.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** With `tool_elicitation = true`, a channel message carrying a registered trigger phrase records a prefilter hit and injects the one-line hint into the latest user message; the same message with the flag unset records no decision and injects nothing. Observed in the linked smoke and pinned by the regressions above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** full-workspace check/clippy/test were not re-run at `c158553d4d` and are left to CI; the scoped runs above cover the touched crates. `bash scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh` was run locally at this head after CI's copy of that job stalled in a network-dependent Telegram test: runtime 3 × 5464 and channels 3 × 1969 passed at 16 threads.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: the hint is new model-visible text, but it is a fixed template parameterized only by the matched tool's registry name — only the untrusted RAW inbound message is scanned — generated channel context and memory enrichment are never scan input — and message text is never echoed into the hint. Telemetry likewise records tool names and trace ids only. A hostile message can at most trigger a hint for a tool the agent already has activated, and the hint explicitly leaves the decision to the model; execution still goes through the normal tool-approval path.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: none required — `tool_elicitation` is a new optional runtime-profile key defaulting to off; existing configs continue to parse. Case- or whitespace-variant tool exclusions now suppress advertisement as well as execution, even with elicitation disabled.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

`git revert <landed-squash-sha>` removes the full change (`risk:medium`). Setting `tool_elicitation = false` (or dropping the key) disables hints once the updated runtime profile is loaded; it does not revert the shared advertisement-exclusion correction.

- **Fast rollback command/path:** disable the profile flag and reload the affected runtime; revert the landed squash commit for full removal
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `runtime_profiles.<name>.tool_elicitation` (default off)
- **Observable failure symptoms:** grep logs for `prefilter_hit` / `hint_injected` with unexpected tool names, or `hint_injected` on turns that should not qualify; user-visible symptom would be the model mentioning a "[tool-hint]" note

prs.title: fix(config): cover Windows profile secrets in default forbidden_paths
prs.body:
## Summary
Windows `default_forbidden_paths()` previously mirrored the Unix secret homes (`~/.gnupg`, `~/.config`) and hard-coded English `C:\Windows` / `Program Files` spellings. Those Unix paths usually do not exist on Windows, and relocated system or profile directories were unprotected.

## Changes
- Resolve `SYSTEMROOT`, `ProgramFiles`, `ProgramFiles(x86)`, `ProgramW6432`, `ProgramData`, and `ProgramFiles(Arm)` from the environment, with English `C:\…` fallbacks.
- Forbid `%APPDATA%\gnupg`, `%APPDATA%\GitHub CLI`, DPAPI / Credential Manager trees, Chromium/Edge `User Data`, and the broader `%APPDATA%` / `%LOCALAPPDATA%` roots (Unix `~/.config` equivalent). Keep `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws`.
- Document the Windows defaults next to the Unix list in `docs/book/src/security/model.md`.
- Unit-test relocated env values and missing-env fallbacks via an injectable getenv helper.

Fixes #12124

- [x] `cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib windows_default_forbidden_paths`

prs.title: fix(delegate): keep a bounded delegate's workspace, tool ceiling and command policy bound beyond the turn (#9872)
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. The head under review is `aa2b45b56`; `master@0f8fb9d37` was merged in by `ba665d125`, `master@be354a7ac` by `abf3896e4` and `master@4e82ce46e` by `a3f7fe257`, so all three are ancestors of the head. `master` has moved on since (`cdefa0d0a` is 2 commits after `4e82ce46e`); `git merge-tree` of the head against it reports no textual conflict, which does not show that the result compiles (the previous head merged cleanly and did not, see *CI*). I have not built that merge. Re-read the head before relying on this line: it names the revision the numbers below were taken on.
- **Problem:** the bounded-delegation contract says the caller bounds what a bounded target can do: its filesystem tools work in the target's own workspace, the caller's tool registry is a ceiling, and the caller's command policy stays authoritative. That bound was applied while the target's turn was assembled and then lost by anything that runs *after* that point, because such work rebuilt its tools or its policy without it. Each escape below is repaired where the bound has to survive, not at the reported symptom.
- **What changed and why:**
  - **Workspace (original scope, #9872).** A bounded delegate's filesystem tools are rebuilt against the target's own policy and workspace. Follow-ups in the same spirit: `git_operations` gets a real command boundary built from the target's sandbox (`DelegateTool::rebuild_target_git_operations_tool`), and `backup`/`data_management` keep the target's policy over `master`'s shared data directory.
  - **Tool ceiling carried into work that outlives the turn.** `SopStepReassembly` carries `caller_allowed`; `all_tools_with_runtime` forwards the ceiling to the scheduler tools and to `spawn_subagent`, which closes the replay of a stored job; `send_message_to_peer` takes a `caller_ceiling` and the entry point it relays through, `process_message_shared_with_live_config_and_admission_and_principal`, an `allowed_tools`, so a relayed peer's turn is capped by the sender's ceiling (including the SOP step that peer starts).
  - **Ceiling derivation.** The sealed ceiling is a set of names, so two stand-ins that report the name of a real capability are excluded at the one place it is sealed: `BoundedSopApproveDenied` (`sop_approve`) and `sub_delegate_tool` (`delegate`). It is sealed after the headless SOP step-scope exclusions.
  - **Deferred shell.** A shell job stores a command, not a tool list, and the scheduler runs it under the owning agent's policy. `require_shell_within_ceiling` refuses `cron_add`'s shell branch, `cron_update`, `schedule` and `cron_run` unless the caller held `shell`; `cron_run` now branches on `job_type`.
  - **Persistence windows.** `cron_update`/`schedule` resume check the ceiling as a `JobGuard` inside the same `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction that commits the write (`cron/store.rs::update_job_inner`), so a concurrent write from another turn of the owning agent cannot land in between. `sop_execute`/`sop_advance` cancel a run they would leave parked (`WaitApproval`, `CheckpointWait`, `Pending`), and so does the live SOP driver at a park it reaches after running a queued step (`QueuedSopAction::bounded_caller`); a cancellation that cannot be persisted is reported, never claimed. The bounded rebind of `sop_execute` records no initiating agent.
  - **Command policy across hops and deferred work (`fe804dd56`).** The maintainer's review of `5758af5b2` asked for this in the PR. The mechanism: *any command a bounded target runs, or leaves behind to run later, under a policy rebuilt one hop below the caller, was judged only by the target's command policy.* The callers' command fields (`autonomy`, `allowed_commands`, `block_high_risk_commands`, `require_approval_for_medium_risk`) now travel inside `SecurityPolicy` as `caller_command_bounds`, root first (`policy.rs:514`, anchor `pub caller_command_bounds: Vec<CallerCommandBound>`), and `validate_command_execution_for_shell` requires a command to clear the policy's own rules and each caller's (`policy.rs:3491`, anchor `for bound in &self.caller_command_bounds`). The chain is attached where the bounded branch of `policy_for_target` already binds budget and cost (`delegate.rs:923`, anchor `target_policy.caller_command_bounds = self.security.caller_command_bounds.clone();`) and inherits the parent's, so hop N is bound by the whole path from the root. Cloning a policy carries it; `ensure_no_escalation_beyond` rejects a child policy that drops one (`policy.rs:4852`, anchor `Err(EscalationViolation::CallerCommandBoundDroppedByChild)`). This replaces the `CallerCommandPolicyShell` wrapper, which gated only the target's direct `shell`.
    - Covered: `cron_add`, `schedule` (`expression`, `delay`, `run_at`), `cron_update` and `cron_run` when a command is written or launched; the STORED command when a job is reused without a command patch (`cron_update` of another field, `schedule` resume), re-judged inside the guarded write (`caller_ceiling.rs:297`, `require_job_within_ceiling`); a `spawn_subagent` child; a second delegation hop, whose "caller" used to be the first target's raw policy.
    - Deferred agent jobs: a bounded registration refuses a stored `allowed_tools` list that keeps `shell`, named or inherited from a ceiling that holds it, at write and at launch or re-arm (`caller_ceiling.rs`, `refuse_deferred_shell` at `:197`). A deferred agent has no command to judge when it is written, so the capability is not deferred.
  - **Review follow-ups after the merge with `master@9cd75ac34`.**

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw lets one agent hand a task to another. In the "bounded" mode the second agent is supposed to stay inside three limits set by the first: it works in its own workspace, it may only use tools the first agent had, and it may only run commands the first agent could run. Those limits held while the second agent's turn was running. They were lost by anything that kept going afterwards: a scheduled job it created, a procedure (SOP) run that was waiting for approval, a message relayed to a peer, a sub-agent it started, or a further hop of delegation. In those cases the work ran later with the full authority of whichever agent owned it.

This PR carries the limits along with that work. A job or run created under a limit is capped by it, a procedure run that would wait for an approval nobody in the turn can follow is cancelled instead, and a command has to satisfy the rules of every agent above it. It adds no capability; it only removes authority that leaked.

What stays the same: agents that are not under a limit behave as before, and jobs already stored are not retroactively capped. The limits listed under "Known boundary", "Second declared gap" and "Third and fourth declared gaps" are not closed here. Only the first has a follow-up issue (#11667); the others are described under *Declared gaps* above and have no issue yet. What operators will notice: a job or run restricted by `allowed_tools` can no longer leave a SOP waiting for approval, and can no longer write SOP definitions through `sop_workshop`.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`: every escape needs a bounded delegation to line up, plus, depending on the case, a peer relay, a concurrent second writer, an externally triggered resume or a further hop. ## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**: this only removes capability from bounded targets and their relayed peers.
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **Yes**
- **Risk and mitigation:** the refusal strings are model-visible. Most are static authored text; `send_message_to_peer: refused — a delegated caller ceiling was declared but never published, so the recipient's turn cannot be bounded` fires only on an internal wiring failure, the same fail-closed contract as `spawn_subagent`'s. The two SOP refusals interpolate values the caller supplied in the same tool call (`sop_execute`'s `name`, `sop_advance`'s `run_id`), each validated against a real SOP definition or run before being echoed, the same class as the existing `require_within_ceiling` echo of stored tool names. Their failure branch also echoes the backend `StoreError`, and the live SOP driver's error echoes an engine-generated run id and the same `StoreError`: backend-internal values, so no new injection surface, with the leak risk (a storage path or driver message in a tool result) of the class already accepted for `require_within_ceiling`. `fe804dd56` adds two strings in `caller_ceiling.rs`: the `refuse_deferred_shell` refusal (static text plus the tool's own name and the literal `shell`) and the stored-command refusal `{tool}: refused — {reason}`, where `reason` is the command policy's message and can echo the stored command text (`Command not allowed by security policy: <command>`). That command was supplied when the job was written and is echoed into a tool result, again the same class. `sop_workshop`'s refusal is static text plus the action's wire name, which comes from a fixed enum (`sop_workshop.rs:208`, anchor `bounded-ceiling-sop-workshop-action`; text in `locales/en/cli.ftl`). The 15 refusals this PR adds render from `bounded-ceiling-*` Fluent keys with their previous English wording, pinned by a test, so that change introduces no new model-visible text.
- **Declared gaps:** see the Known boundary, the Second declared gap and the Third and fourth declared gaps under *Declared gaps*: the command chain does not reach a peer relay or a cross-agent SOP step, a principal-narrowed `Agent` session's scheduler tools carry no sealed ceiling, a SOP step's ceiling is the caller's raw list, and the seal's inputs at its two call sites are not pinned by a test.   - a bounded caller's `sop_execute`/`sop_advance`, and the live SOP driver after a queued step, cancel a run that would park (approval, checkpoint, unmet dependency) instead of leaving it resumable with full authority; a bounded rebind of `sop_execute` records no initiating agent;

  - `backup`/`data_management` follow `master`'s shared data directory under the target's policy;
  - every command a bounded target runs, or stores to run later, must also clear the command policy of each caller above it, at every bounded hop and for a `spawn_subagent` child; a command the caller's policy refuses is refused even if the target's profile allows it;
  - a bounded registration cannot store, launch or re-arm an agent job whose `allowed_tools` keeps `shell`, and `schedule` resume reads the request's `approved` like the create routes. A job already stored with `shell` stays stored, but a bounded turn cannot launch or re-arm it;
  - a command denied by both the target's and a caller's policy reports the target's message;
  - any `agent::run` given a per-run `allowed_tools` (a stored cron agent job with its own list, for example) now builds its scheduler tools with a ceiling sealed to the tools that run actually holds (the list intersected with its assembled registry), so a job it stores or launches is capped by it and an agent job that keeps `shell` is refused (`agent/loop_.rs:1735`, anchor `crate::tools::caller_ceiling::seal_to_registry(`, and `cron/scheduler.rs:1180`, anchor `job.allowed_tools.clone()`). Read from the code.
  - `sop_workshop` keeps only `list` and `inspect` under a caller ceiling, and `sop_execute`/`sop_advance` cancel a run that would park in every registry built with one: a bounded target, a restricted `agent::run` (so a `spawn_subagent` child and a cron-fired job) and a peer relay; a SOP step turn never holds these two tools, because the step scope excludes them by name. Under a ceiling `sop_execute` also records no initiating agent. This includes a job whose `allowed_tools` an operator wrote: such a job can no longer leave a SOP waiting for approval or write SOP definitions, so a job that has to do either must not be restricted by `allowed_tools`. An RPC principal session restricted by tool names builds its registry with no ceiling and is not covered (see the Second declared gap).

  - a turn given a per-run `allowed_tools` seals its ceiling to the tools it actually holds (plus the deferred MCP tools it may activate, and, when its set does not name `tool_search`, the ones a `mode = "always"` group already activated), not to the names it was handed: a name its own policy removed no longer counts as held, for example `shell` for a peer whose profile has none;
  - a bounded delegate's rebuilt tools read the config the delegation was admitted against, so a feature switched on or off in that config is seen by the target;
  - a nested bounded hop is handed only the MCP tools its own bundles grant;
  - the 15 refusals added by this PR render from Fluent keys; in a locale without a translation they stay English.

  Jobs already stored under the old, wider ceiling are **not** retro-capped, and a SOP run already left parked before this is deployed is not retroactively cancelled.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the commits on this branch, or revert the PR merge commit. No migration or state cleanup: nothing persisted changed shape.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. The bound is active whenever a ceiling is in force.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a legitimate scheduled job stops being created, re-armed or launched; a legitimate `sop_approve`/`delegate` capability stops surviving into a stored job; a legitimate peer relay stops receiving a tool the peer's own profile grants; a legitimate concurrent job update starts losing to a rival write; a SOP run started by a bounded caller is cancelled instead of resumable; a bounded target's command is refused that its own profile allows. Grep tool results for:
  - `refused — this stores or re-arms a shell job` (`cron_add`, `cron_update`, `schedule`, `cron_run`)
  - `refused — this job's stored allowed_tools reach beyond` and `refused — this job stores no allowed_tools`
  - `refused — this agent job would keep 'shell'`: a bounded registration tried to defer an agent with `shell`; the job has to list its tools without it
  - `<tool>: refused — ... Command not allowed by security policy` from `cron_update` or `schedule` resume: a caller's policy refuses the job's stored command; check the caller's `allowed_commands` before treating it as a regression
  - `refused — this tool was registered under bounded delegation but the caller's tool ceiling was never sealed`, and `send_message_to_peer: refused — a delegated caller ceiling was declared but never published`: fail-closed paths that indicate a sealing bug, not a policy decision
  - `refused — SOP` / `refused — run ... left outside this turn ... has been cancelled` (`sop_execute`, `sop_advance`): the parked-run cancellation path
  - ``sop_workshop `<action>` is not available under a caller tool ceiling``: the `sop_workshop` write refusal (`propose`, `capture_run`, `apply`, `reject`, `quarantine`); `list` and `inspect` are unaffected
  - `could NOT be cancelled ... may still be active - treat it as unresolved, not closed`: the cancellation failed to persist, the run is still parked and resumable; investigate the persistence backend
  - log line `bounded live SOP driver: cancelled a run that would have parked outside the turn`; its unpersisted counterpart `bounded live SOP driver: parked run could not be cancelled` comes with a turn error containing `reached a park that a bounded caller's tool ceiling cannot follow past this turn`
  - a cron job update or resume that fails with no obvious cause: check for a concurrent write from another turn of the same agent; it now surfaces as lock contention or a guard refusal instead of silently winning or losing
  - From `1a328ea53` the refusal strings above come from the `bounded-ceiling-*` keys in `locales/en/cli.ftl`; in a locale without a translation they stay the English text quoted here.

prs.title: feat(transcription): add default_provider fallback for agents without a transcription alias
prs.body:
## Problem

`TranscriptionManager::transcribe()` fails loud when the runtime agent has no `transcription_provider` configured — there is deliberately no global default. In practice this means voice transcription silently (well, loudly) does nothing for every agent until each one is given its own alias, even when the deployment has exactly one transcription provider and the operator considers it deployment-wide.

## Change

- New optional `[transcription].default_provider`: when set, agents without their own `transcription_provider` fall back to it; agents with their own alias are unaffected. When neither is set, the existing fail-loud behavior is unchanged.
- `TranscriptionManager` gains `resolved_agent_alias()` (agent alias → `default_provider` → empty); `transcribe()` dispatches through it, and the unbound-agent error now points at `[transcription].default_provider` as the remediation.
- The voice path in `telegram.rs` resolves via the same API (`transcribe_with_provider`), keeping its warn-and-skip disposition when nothing is bound.
- The V2→V3 migration used to drop the legacy `[transcription].default_provider` key as having no V3 home; it now carries through, since V3 gains the field back under the same name.

Note: `TranscriptionManager::new`/`from_sections` take the new value as a parameter (all in-repo call sites updated). Happy to switch to reading it from `TranscriptionConfig` inside the constructor if the maintainers prefer a smaller public diff.

## Tests

- `resolved_agent_alias_prefers_agent_then_default_then_empty`
- `transcribe_dispatches_to_agent_alias_when_set` (no behavior change)
- `transcribe_falls_back_to_default_provider_when_agent_unbound`
- `transcribe_fails_loud_when_agent_unbound_and_no_default_provider`
- `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib transcription` — 76 passed, 0 failed; `cargo check -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels` clean.

prs.title: fix(memory): make markdown store() writes append-only to stop concurrent lost updates
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `MarkdownMemory::append_to_file` (the function `store()`/`store_with_agent`/the default-trait `store_with_metadata`/`store_with_options*` all end up calling) used to read the whole file, append in memory, and rewrite it with a truncating `fs::write`. Two overlapping `store()` calls — same process, independent `MarkdownMemory` instances over the same workspace, or separate host processes — could each read before the other's write landed, so one call's row silently vanished even though both returned `Ok`.
  - A read failure (e.g. invalid UTF-8 left by an earlier partial write) was coerced to `""` by `unwrap_or_default()`, so the very next `store()` replaced the whole file with just its own row — deterministic, no concurrency needed.
  - The fix removes the read entirely: it opens the file for append and issues one `write_all`, so the row lands at the current end regardless of what else is writing. The first `store()` against a missing file uses a create-new-exclusive open (`O_CREAT | O_EXCL`) so exactly one caller creates the file; every other concurrent first-write loses that race and appends its row instead of truncating the winner's file.
- **Scope boundary:** this PR only changes `MarkdownMemory::append_to_file` (the `store()` write path) and adds regression tests. It does **not** touch the other code that replaces a markdown memory file wholesale instead of appending to it — including, but not limited to: personality-preset seeding (`agent/personality_templates/mod.rs`), the personality `put` RPC and its gateway endpoint (`rpc/dispatch.rs`, `gateway/api_personality.rs`), the `file_edit`/`file_write` tools, the dashboard explorer's delete/move of `memory/` paths (`runtime/src/browse.rs`; `memory/` is not in `AGENT_WORKSPACE_PROTECTED_DIRS`), memory-file hygiene archival/purge, agent-rename, backup restore, and alias import. Those replace-or-remove-the-whole-file mechanisms need a different approach (compare-and-swap on mtime/hash, or serialization) and a product decision this issue doesn't make. Related: #11136 (closed) covers the same lost-update failure class for parallel `file_edit`/`file_write` calls on one path within a single tool batch — a different mechanism, not `MarkdownMemory::store()`.
- **Blast radius:** every caller that reaches `MarkdownMemory::store`/`store_with_agent`/the trait-default `store_with_metadata`/`store_with_options*` on the markdown backend goes through the fixed function, including (not an exhaustive list) the `memory_store` tool, the gateway's memory HTTP endpoint, the runtime's `memory` RPC, SOP audit logging, agent/orchestrator per-turn and autosave paths, Discord channel archival, and the decorators `AgentScopedMarkdownMemory` → `ScannedMemory` → `AuditedMemory` → `RetrievalPipeline` that wrap a markdown backend end to end. `recall`/`list`/`count` and the dashboard explorer's *read* paths are unaffected (no code change there); the explorer's delete/move of workspace paths is unaffected too but is not a reader, it's a separate writer out of scope (see above).
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #10797. Related #11136.

### What this does, simply

Markdown memory (`MEMORY.md` and the daily log files) is supposed to be append-only: every `store()` call should just add a row and never erase one that already landed. The old code didn't actually append — it read the file, glued the new row on in memory, and wrote the whole thing back. If two `store()` calls happened to overlap (two memory-store tool calls in one turn, two concurrent conversation turns on the same agent, a daemon and a CLI process, two delegate workers), whichever call's rewrite landed last would silently discard whatever the other one had just added, even though both calls reported success. And if the file couldn't be read at all (for example because an earlier crash left some invalid bytes in it), the code treated that exactly like an empty file and replaced everything in it with just the new entry.

This PR changes the write itself so there is no read to race against: it opens the file in append mode and writes the new row in one call, so the operating system places it after whatever is already there no matter who else is writing at the same time. Three things change as a direct result, because deciding any of them would require reading the file first, which is exactly what this fix removes:

- If `MEMORY.md` is a dangling symlink, `store()` now fails instead of silently creating a file wherever the symlink happened to point. A symlink that points at a real file is still followed exactly as before.
- If `MEMORY.md` already exists but is empty, the next `store()` no longer adds the `# Long-Term Memory` header — it just appends the row. (A brand-new file still gets the header, via a create-new-exclusive open that only one concurrent first writer can win.)
- A file holding invalid bytes from an earlier failure is never read, so a `store()` against it can no longer be mistaken for "empty" and overwritten — the new row is appended after the old bytes, untouched.

Known, cosmetic-only limitation: when several `store()` calls race to create a brand-new file, the winner's create-and-write is two separate steps, so a loser can occasionally append its row in between and end up *before* the header rather than after it. No row is ever lost, and the code that reads these files already ignores every line starting with `#` no matter where it sits, so `recall`/`list`/`count` see no difference. It's documented at the call site (`crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/markdown.rs`) rather than fixed here; see "Testing" below for how it was measured, and "Alternatives considered" for why a true fix was judged not worth the extra code for a cosmetic, non-lossy edge case.

### Alternatives considered for the header-ordering limitation

- **Document it (chosen).** Correct the misleading in-code comment and declare the limitation here. No new code, no new failure mode; the existing test suite already demonstrates it causes no data loss or misread entries.
- **Atomic create via temp file + `hard_link`.** Write the full header+content to a temp file in the same directory, then `std::fs::hard_link` it into place; on `AlreadyExists`, delete the temp file and fall back to append. Would genuinely close the window, at the cost of more code (and a temp file to clean up on every exit path) for a bug that loses no data.
- **Temp file + `rename` — rejected.** `rename` onto an existing destination replaces it atomically on POSIX. If a loser's append already landed in the destination while the winner is building its temp file, the winner's `rename` would silently destroy that row — strictly worse than the bug it would fix.
- **Advisory file lock around create+write — not pursued.** Would need a new dependency (`fs2`/`fd-lock`, not currently in `Cargo.lock`) for a once-per-file race with no data loss.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — this is a library-level fix with no user-facing interface; the behavior is exercised directly by the regression tests below, which reproduce the exact shapes described in the issue.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required `lint` job (`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`) and the crate's own test job cover this diff directly; both were also run locally against the final commit (below) because `clippy` on Windows cannot reach `zeroclaw-memory` at all under `-D warnings` (unrelated pre-existing warnings in `zeroclaw-config` fail first), so the authoritative clippy run for this change was done on Linux.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the dangling-symlink behavior change is now covered by a `#[cfg(unix)]` test (symlink creation needs no privilege on Linux); it was not independently re-verified on Windows because this dev machine lacks the privilege to create a test symlink (`os error 1314`), and CI's Windows job does not create symlinks in a privileged context either. Windows users get the same `create_new`-refuses-an-existing-path behavior by construction (one code path, no `#[cfg]` split), but that specific claim rests on reading the Windows `CREATE_NEW` semantics, not on a Windows-side test run.
- **Commands run and tail output** (final commit, both platforms):

  Linux (WSL, Ubuntu 24.04), authoritative for clippy and for the new `#[cfg(unix)]` test:
  ```
  $ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-memory --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
      Checking zeroclaw-memory v0.8.6 (.../zeroclaw-memory)
      Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 14.91s

  $ cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --locked -- --test-threads=4
  test result: ok. 561 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out   (--lib)
  test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out     (tests/agent_migration.rs)
  test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out     (tests/markdown_concurrent_store.rs)
  test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out     (doc-tests)
  ```
  The one `--lib` ignore is `sqlite_permissions::tests::sqlite_storage_lock_probe`, a pre-existing subprocess probe unrelated to this diff.

  Windows (MSVC), `--lib`:
  ```
  $ cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --locked -- --test-threads=4
  test result: FAILED. 534 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
  ```
  The one failure is `sqlite_permissions::portable_tests::sqlite_storage_rejects_windows_symlink_leaves`, which panics with "requires symlink privileges: Os { code: 1314 }" — a pre-existing environment limitation in a file this diff does not touch, reproducible on `origin/master` with no changes at all.

  `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean for both files in this diff.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - That the 4 new/changed unit tests and both new integration tests actually fail against the pre-fix code, not just pass against the fix: temporarily reverted `append_to_file`'s body to the `origin/master` read-modify-write logic (tests untouched) and re-ran. Result: `store_adds_no_header_to_an_existing_but_empty_file`, `store_keeps_prior_bytes_when_existing_file_is_not_valid_utf8`, `concurrent_stores_from_independent_instances_lose_no_row`, and `concurrent_first_stores_write_one_header_and_every_row` (unit tests) and both tests in `markdown_concurrent_store.rs` fail; `store_keeps_the_established_file_format` passes on both (it only checks sequential, non-racing output, which the fix doesn't change). Restored the fix afterward and reran to confirm a clean tree (`git diff HEAD --stat` empty) and a green suite.
  - The UTF-8 and empty-file cases fail deterministically on every run; the two concurrency tests are probabilistic — they failed on every run observed in this session, but are not guaranteed to fail on different hardware or thread counts.
  - The header-ordering limitation described above: a temporary, throwaway test (not included in this PR) ran 200 rounds of 16 concurrent first-`store()`s against the fixed code on this branch: `header_not_first=9/200 rows_lost_rounds=0/200`. This is what "cosmetic-only, documented rather than fixed" is based on.
  - That a symlink pointing at a real file is still followed by both the old and the new code (no behavior change there) — read, not asserted in a test, since it was already true before this PR and isn't part of the bug.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A` — no user-visible interface changed.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** final commit on `fix/10797-markdown-append-only`; no rendered interface involved.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** see command tails above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** see "Beyond CI" above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** did not run the full workspace test suite or `zeroclaw-runtime`/`zeroclaw-gateway`/`zeroclaw-channels` integration tests; the diff is contained to one function in `zeroclaw-memory` plus its own tests, and the required CI covers the broader workspace.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No` — same file, same directory, same open modes' effective scope as before (append/create vs. read+write); no new paths touched.
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`, with three documented edge-case behavior changes (dangling symlink now errors; existing-empty file no longer gets a retroactive header; a file with invalid UTF-8 is no longer read-and-possibly-replaced, since it's never read at all) — see "What this does, simply". Normal sequential, single-writer usage against a well-formed file is unaffected.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`

## Rollback

This issue carries `risk:high`/`priority:p1` labels, which describe the *bug's* impact (silent, unattributed data loss). The risk of *this fix* is narrower: it changes one function's I/O strategy, adds no new write paths or dependencies, and every edge-case behavior change is covered by a dedicated test. On that basis this PR is low-risk and `git revert <sha>` is the rollback plan; reverting restores the old read-modify-write behavior (and its lost-update bug) with no migration needed, since the on-disk file format is unchanged.

prs.title: fix(runtime): restore agent_alias attribution on cron/gateway agent runs
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** cron- and gateway-triggered agent runs emitted the tool/provider/turn records of the run body without `agent_alias` (only `cron_job_id` / `risk_profile` survived). Root cause: `agent::run` and `process_message_inner` build the run body as `body.instrument(scope_span).instrument(attribution_span)`, but the log layer walks *recorded span parents* — the scope span is created eagerly in the prologue, so it records the caller context as its parent and the agent attribution span never enters the walked chain.
- Fix: name the attribution span as the scope span's parent (`parent: &__zc_attribution_span`) in both call sites, with a comment explaining the mechanism so the pattern is not reintroduced.
- Regression test `run_body_scope_span_keeps_agent_attribution_reachable` mirrors the production wiring and asserts `agent_alias` + `risk_profile` reach an event emitted from a nested tool span.
- **Scope boundary:** no change to span creation in the channel orchestrator (its lazily-entered scope spans are correct); no changes to cron scheduling/delivery or to the log merge algorithm itself.
- **Blast radius:** observability consumers only. Cron-run events now carry `zc_role: "agent"` (nearest attribution wins by design) alongside the preserved `cron_job_id`; consumers that filter cron runs by `zc_role == "cron"` should filter by presence of `cron_job_id` instead.
- **Linked issues:** none open for this exact defect.

### What this does, simply

Every log event is signed with the agent that produced it by walking the chain of recorded span parents, leaf to root, and merging attribution found along the way. Cron and gateway runs assembled their span stack in a way that silently cut the agent label out of that chain: the "small" scope span was stamped with the caller as its parent before the "big" agent-attribution span was placed around the body, so events emitted under the scope span walked past the agent label and found only the outer cron label. The result was fully anonymous cron runs — tool failures no monitoring rule could attribute to an agent, per-agent metrics missing for every non-channel run. The fix stamps the scope span with the attribution span as its parent at creation, so the walked chain is whole: events carry the agent alias again, and the cron job id is retained next to it.

Verified in production A/B on our own deployment: pre-fix cron run of a worker agent — ~200 events, none with `agent_alias`; post-fix run — all 52 events carry `agent_alias` + `cron_job_id`, including a failed tool call that previously would have been an anonymous failure record.

## Testing (required)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — the regression test covers the wiring; the change is invisible to interactive surfaces and the pre/post delta is shown by the regression test and the A/B evidence above.
- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** required CI (`Test`, `Lint`, `Format`, clippy) — the changed surface is zeroclaw-runtime, covered by the workspace test matrix.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none known.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  ```sh
  cargo fmt --all -- --check
  cargo check -p zeroclaw-runtime --tests   # exit 0 (pre-existing unrelated warnings only)
  ```
  Additionally, a standalone probe against the real `zeroclaw-log`/`zeroclaw-api` path dependencies reproduced the defect on the old wiring (`agent_alias: null`) and confirmed attribution on the fixed wiring (`{"agent_alias":"probe_agent","risk_profile":"probe-risk","tool":"probe_tool","zc_role":"agent"}`).
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Production A/B before/after deploying the patch: cron-run events of a live worker agent transitioned from fully anonymous to fully attributed, with `cron_job_id` preserved. Not verified: channel-path regression (its span wiring is untouched and covered by existing tests).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no user-visible interface state changed.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** revision `039287065`; evidence: JSONL runtime trace events of a cron-spawned agent run.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** full `cargo test` of zeroclaw-runtime not run locally (long compile); the new regression test is exercised by required CI.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No**

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Yes** (log schema gains no new keys; `agent_alias` populates where it was previously absent)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **No**
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No**

## Rollback

`git revert <sha>` — the change is two `parent:` arguments plus a test; revert restores the previous (buggy) attribution behavior with no other effect.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - A native runtime whose shell is absent (the shell-free distroless `latest` image) advertised POSIX shell access, registered the `shell` tool and told the model it had `sh`, while every command could only fail. With an injected PATH (TUI/ACP) the factory instead failed agent construction.
  - An absent shell is now a missing capability: `NativeRuntime` reports `ShellDialect::None`; `build_shell_command` (and the effective-PATH variant) fail closed; and `shell`, `schedule` and skill `shell`/`script` tools are not registered. `NativeRuntime::new()` and both factory paths decide the same way.
  - "Absent" means every absolute PATH entry (or the absolute `runtime.shell`) was probed and reported `NotFound` or `NotADirectory` (`shell_is_absent`), not the resolver's error kind: the resolver reports the error of *another* PATH entry when the shell is nowhere to be found. Any other probe failure (for example `PermissionDenied` on an unsearchable directory, or a symlink loop in a parent component) does not prove absence: the shell stays "not absent" and the resolver reports its error as before (a construction error with an injected PATH, a failure when the command is built with the ambient PATH).
  - A malformed `runtime.shell` (empty, relative) is still a construction error, and a shell that exists but is unusable (not executable, a directory, a dangling symlink) keeps its earlier behavior.
  - The new shell-absence tests are skipped on Android (`not(target_os = "android")`): it pins `/system/bin/sh` and never reports the shell absent.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - Does not add a shell to the image, and does not add the release-container regression test requested in the triage of #9859 (a CI change; follow-up).
  - Does not change Windows, Android or Docker runtime behavior (new code is `cfg(unix)`).
  - Still offering shell-dependent surface without a shell, failing closed through `policy.rs` (`ShellDialect::None` → high risk): `cron_add` / `cron_update` / `cron_run` advertise `job_type: "shell"` (they also create agent jobs). Removing `schedule` also removes its list/cancel/pause actions.
  - Out of this mechanism: `bedrock.rs` and `skills/testing.rs` spawn `sh` directly, not through `RuntimeAdapter`.
  - `with_shell(...)` stays unchecked on purpose (explicit shell, used by tests).
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw-config` platform factory and `NativeRuntime`; tool registration in `zeroclaw-runtime` (`all_tools_with_runtime`, `default_tools_with_runtime`, skill tool preparation). Any runtime reporting `ShellDialect::None` no longer registers `shell`; I did not verify whether the wasm runtime reaches these registries.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #9859 (not closing it: the container regression test is not included).

### What this does, simply

The official `latest` image has no shell on purpose. Since #10381 the daemon no longer refuses to start without one, but it still told the model it could run shell commands, offered the `shell` tool, and every call failed. This PR makes the runtime say the truth: no shell was found, so shell commands are not offered and any attempt to build one fails with a clear message. Chat turns that need no shell are unaffected.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — covered by the unit and integration tests below; a release-container check is the follow-up left in #9859.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** required CI for `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-runtime`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** no test runs the distroless image; Windows and Android were not built locally.
- **Commands run and tail output:** (WSL Ubuntu 24.04, `-j 1`; head `bca6fd9d7`, which merges `master` `7f39e313e`)
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- platform::` → `83 passed; 0 failed` (on `bca6fd9d7`)
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --test native_shell_absent_ambient_path` → `1 passed` (on `bca6fd9d7`)
  - `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh` → pass (on `bca6fd9d7`)
  - On `6afbbcf24`: `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib -- skills:: tools::` → `1104 passed`; `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib` and `--tests` with `-D warnings`, and `cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime` → clean. `bca6fd9d7` only changes tests in `zeroclaw-config`; I did not re-run the runtime commands on it.
  - Earlier runs on `fd9d131a3` / merge commit `809ce20b3` (`cron:: platform:: security::` → `1715 passed`; `agent:: rpc:: sop:: composition::` → `3060 passed`; `scripts/ci/container_build_inputs_gate.sh`, `scripts/dev/act-local.test.sh`) were not repeated.
  - Negative controls: the new tests fail against the earlier probe that read any error as absent (3 failures in `platform::`); the registry and skills controls from before are unchanged.
  - The permission tests (`0o000` directory) return early with a `skipped:` note on stderr when the process runs as root, because permissions are not enforced there. libtest and nextest hide that note for passing tests unless output capture is disabled. Not built or run: Android, Windows.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** On unpatched `master` (`9dbb57231`), with a PATH that contains no `sh`, a throwaway test showed `create_runtime` returning `Ok` with `has_shell_access = true`, profile `sh`, and `build_shell_command` failing. Not verified: a real `/webhook` request, the distroless image itself, Windows/Android builds, `gateway` and `channels` tests. No test plants a relative-PATH decoy (the resolver's handling of relative entries is covered in `executable.rs`; `set_current_dir` is disallowed by clippy here).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (no user-visible interface state).
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** full-workspace test/clippy skipped for memory limits on the dev machine.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No — the system prompt no longer names a shell when none exists.
- The change only removes capability. Resolution still considers absolute PATH entries only (`executable.rs`), and `shell_is_absent` does the same, so an unresolved shell is never searched for in the workspace (the rule from #10381).

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes, with one behavior change: an injected PATH (TUI/ACP) that is empty, relative-only or lacks the shell used to fail agent construction; it now yields an agent without `shell`/`schedule` and a single WARN per process (a prior status read may have used it up).
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- The no-shell state is computed when the runtime is built, so installing a shell afterwards needs a config reload.
- Trade-off of that rule: probing stops at the first entry that cannot be probed, so a host whose PATH has an unsearchable entry before a readable one that holds the shell is also reported "not absent" (the resolver then decides). That keeps the diagnostic instead of reporting a missing shell.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a one-time WARN `native runtime shell was not found; shell commands are unavailable`; a missing `shell` tool on a host that does have a shell would indicate a wrong "absent" decision.
